about: Feedback loop builder (docs/anp-spec.md section 8.3). Each loop fills the seven slots every loop in the course uses: Stimulus, Receptor (sensor), Afferent pathway, Control center, Efferent pathway, Effector, Response. Each slot has the card text, a short label for the finished diagram, and why it belongs there. Distractor cards belong in no slot. Then the learner classifies the loop (kind) and predicts the effect of a failed part. "map" names the dependency-map loop this one fulfils. Item ids: feedback-loops:<loop>:<slot>, :kind and :failure. Checked by scripts/lib/anp-tool-checks/feedback-loops.mjs.

loops.title: Body temperature falls
loops.map: Generic loop anatomy: stimulus to response (introduces every slot)
loops.scenario: You step outside on a winter morning at −5 °C. Within a minute your fingers go pale and you start to shiver, and your body temperature stays close to 37 °C.

stimulus.text: Cold air cools your skin and blood
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the change in the regulated variable: here, temperature falling below its set point.

sensor.text: Cold-sensitive nerve endings in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the brain
sensor.why: These sensory receptors detect the fall. Cold-sensitive endings in the skin fire more as the skin cools.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries information toward the control center. Here that is sensory nerves carrying action potentials.

control.text: Temperature control center in the brain
control.why: The control center compares the incoming temperature with the set point and sends out commands.

efferent.text: Nerves to skin blood vessels and skeletal muscles
efferent.why: The efferent pathway carries commands away from the control center, here as nerve signals.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of skin blood vessels, and skeletal muscles
effector.why: Effectors carry out the commands. Smooth muscle narrows the skin vessels; skeletal muscles contract in rapid small bursts (shivering).

response.text: Skin vessels constrict to keep heat in, and muscles shiver to release heat, so body temperature rises back toward the set point
response.short: Heat kept in and made: temperature rises
response.why: Vasoconstriction keeps warm blood away from the skin, and the rapid bursts of muscle contraction release heat. Both push temperature back up, opposing the fall.

distractors.text: Sweat glands release sweat
distractors.why: Sweat carries heat away. That is a response for when temperature rises, the opposite of what this loop needs.

distractors.text: The set point is lowered to match the cold
distractors.why: The set point stays where it is. The loop works by pushing temperature back toward it.

distractors.text: Warm-sensitive nerve endings fire faster
distractors.why: Cooling makes warm-sensitive endings fire less, not more. The cold-sensitive endings are the ones signaling here.

loops.classify: The response (heat kept in and made) opposes the stimulus (a fall in temperature), so this is negative feedback. As temperature returns toward the set point, the stimulus shrinks and the loop eases off by itself.

failure.q: An 85-year-old’s skin vessels constrict weakly and their muscles shiver weakly: the effectors are weakened. What happens during a long cold day outdoors?

options.text: Body temperature drifts below normal as the weak response falls behind
options.why: Right. The sensors, pathways and control center all work, but the loop can only correct as much as its effectors can deliver. This is why older adults are more at risk when they get very cold.

options.text: Body temperature stays normal, because the control center lowers the set point instead
options.why: The control center does not move the set point to excuse a failing response. It keeps sending commands the effectors cannot fully carry out.

options.text: Body temperature rises, because weak effectors make the sensors misread the cold as heat
options.why: Nothing in this failure affects the sensors. They still detect cold correctly.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the sensors still detect the cold
options.why: Detecting a change is not enough. Without a strong enough response, the variable is not pushed back.

loops.title: Body temperature rises
loops.scenario: You run for half an hour on a warm afternoon. Your skin flushes and you sweat, and your body temperature settles just above 37 °C instead of climbing.

stimulus.text: Exercise and warm air raise your body temperature
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a rise in the regulated variable above its set point. Working muscles release heat faster than it is lost.

sensor.text: Warm-sensitive nerve endings in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the brain
sensor.why: These sensory receptors fire more as they warm, detecting the rise.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries the information toward the control center.

control.text: Temperature control center in the brain
control.why: The control center compares the higher temperature with the set point and sends out commands.

efferent.text: Nerves to skin blood vessels and to sweat glands
efferent.short: Nerves to vessels and sweat glands
efferent.why: The efferent pathway carries the commands out, here as nerve signals.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of skin blood vessels, and sweat glands
effector.why: The smooth muscle relaxes to widen the vessels, and the glands release sweat.

response.text: Skin vessels dilate so more heat leaves, and sweat evaporates and carries heat away, so body temperature falls back toward the set point
response.why: More warm blood near the surface and evaporating sweat both remove heat, opposing the rise.

distractors.text: Skeletal muscles shiver
distractors.why: Shivering releases heat. That would make the rise worse, so it belongs to the loop for falling temperature.

distractors.text: Skin vessels constrict to keep warm blood in
distractors.why: Constriction holds heat in. It is the response to cold, the opposite of what is needed here.

distractors.text: Cold-sensitive nerve endings fire faster
distractors.why: Warming makes cold-sensitive endings fire less. The warm-sensitive endings detect this rise.

loops.classify: The response (heat lost) opposes the stimulus (a rise in temperature), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: On a very humid day, sweat drips off instead of evaporating, so the sweat removes little heat. What happens to body temperature during a long run?

options.text: It keeps rising as heat is made faster than it is lost
options.why: Right. The loop detects the rise and commands the sweat glands to release sweat, but sweat cools only when it evaporates. If heat is made faster than it is lost, temperature climbs, which is how exertional heat illness develops.

options.text: It stays normal, because the sweat glands simply release more sweat
options.why: More sweat does not help if it cannot evaporate. It drips away and takes water, not heat, with it.

options.text: It falls, because the skin vessels dilate
options.why: Dilation moves heat to the skin, but on a hot, humid day the skin cannot shed it fast enough to lower body temperature.

options.text: It stays normal, because the set point moves up to match
options.why: Exercise does not move the set point. The control center keeps trying to bring temperature down to the same target.

loops.title: Glucose in the blood rises after a meal
loops.scenario: An hour after a large bowl of pasta, glucose absorbed from your gut has pushed up the glucose level in your blood. Two hours later it is back near its usual level.

stimulus.text: Glucose in your blood rises after a meal
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the rise in a regulated variable, the concentration of glucose in the blood.

sensor.text: Gland cells in the pancreas detect the rise
sensor.why: Some gland cells in the pancreas are themselves the sensor: they respond directly to the glucose level of the blood flowing past them.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the sensing cells are the deciding cells
afferent.why: Here the sensor and the control center are the same cells, so the afferent pathway is as short as it can be. No nerve is needed.

control.text: The same pancreas gland cells set how much hormone to release
control.why: These cells compare the glucose level with their set point and release more hormone the higher it is.

efferent.text: A hormone carried in the blood
efferent.why: The command travels as a chemical messenger in the blood. An efferent pathway does not have to be a nerve.

effector.text: Liver, muscle and fat cells
effector.why: These target cells have receptor proteins for the hormone and respond by taking up glucose.

response.text: Cells take up and store glucose, so the glucose level falls back toward the set point
response.why: Glucose moves out of the blood into cells, opposing the rise.

distractors.text: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain
distractors.why: This loop needs no nerve: the pancreas cells sense the glucose themselves and respond directly.

distractors.text: A hormone that raises the glucose level
distractors.why: That is the between-meals loop. After a meal the pancreas releases the hormone that lowers glucose.

distractors.text: Glucose is released from the liver into the blood
distractors.why: That would push glucose further up, the opposite of what this loop does.

loops.classify: The response (glucose leaves the blood) opposes the stimulus (a rise in the glucose level), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: Suppose the pancreas gland cells still detect the rise in glucose but can no longer make the hormone that lowers it. What happens after meals?

options.text: The glucose level rises and stays high, because the command never reaches the cells
options.why: Right. The rise is detected, but with no hormone the efferent pathway is broken, so the effectors never get the signal.

options.text: The glucose level stays normal, because the liver, muscle and fat cells sense the glucose themselves
options.why: Those cells are effectors, not sensors. They take up glucose in response to the hormone, which is now missing.

options.text: The glucose level falls too low, because nothing stops the loop
options.why: With no hormone, nothing drives glucose into the cells, so the level cannot fall.

options.text: The glucose level stays normal, because the brain takes over as the control center
options.why: The brain is not part of this loop. There is no other path for the command to take.

loops.title: Blood oxygen is low
loops.scenario: You move to a mountain town where each breath brings in less oxygen. Over the next few weeks, your blood slowly gains more red blood cells.

stimulus.text: Your blood carries too little oxygen
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a fall in the oxygen the blood delivers to tissues.

sensor.text: Cells in the kidneys detect the low oxygen
sensor.why: Specialized kidney cells respond directly to the oxygen level in the blood reaching them.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the kidney cells that sense also respond
afferent.why: The sensing cells and the deciding cells are the same, so no nerve carries the information.

control.text: The same kidney cells set how much hormone to release
control.why: The lower the oxygen, the more hormone these cells release.

efferent.text: A hormone carried in the blood
efferent.why: The command travels in the blood to a distant target.

effector.text: Bone marrow
effector.why: This tissue responds to the hormone by producing red blood cells faster.

response.text: More red blood cells are made, the blood carries more oxygen, and the signal fades
response.why: More red blood cells carry more oxygen, which removes the stimulus.

distractors.text: The lungs breathe faster
distractors.why: Faster breathing is a separate, quick response controlled by the brain. This loop works through the kidneys and a hormone, over days to weeks.

distractors.text: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain
distractors.why: No nerve is involved: the kidney cells sense oxygen and release the hormone themselves.

distractors.text: Fewer red blood cells are made
distractors.why: Fewer red cells would carry even less oxygen, pushing the variable further from its set point.

loops.classify: The response (more oxygen carried) opposes the stimulus (too little oxygen), so this is negative feedback. As oxygen recovers, hormone release falls again.

failure.q: Badly damaged kidneys make very little of the hormone, even when oxygen is low. What happens to the red blood cell count?

options.text: It falls and stays low, because the bone marrow never gets the command to make more
options.why: Right. Red cells wear out and are replaced only as fast as the hormone drives production. With the efferent pathway broken, the count drifts down.

options.text: It rises, because the low oxygen acts on the bone marrow directly
options.why: The bone marrow responds to the hormone, not to oxygen itself. Without the hormone, production slows.

options.text: It stays normal, because the lungs make up for it
options.why: The lungs cannot make red blood cells. Breathing faster does not replace the missing hormone.

options.text: It stays normal, because the sensor still detects low oxygen
options.why: Detection alone does nothing if the command cannot be sent.

loops.title: Contractions in childbirth
loops.scenario: Late in labor, contractions come harder and closer together, each one pushing the baby further down, until the baby is born.

stimulus.text: The baby’s head stretches the lower opening of the uterus
stimulus.why: The stimulus is stretch of the lower opening of the uterus.

sensor.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the lower uterus
sensor.why: These sensory receptors fire more as the opening stretches.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carry signals to the brain
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries the stretch information to the brain.

control.text: The brain
control.why: The brain is the control center: more stretch signals lead to more hormone release.

efferent.text: The pituitary gland releases a hormone into the blood
efferent.why: The command travels as a hormone released from the pituitary gland into the blood.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of the uterus
effector.why: The hormone makes the smooth muscle of the uterus contract harder.

response.text: Stronger contractions push the head down further, stretching the opening even more
response.why: The response increases the very stimulus that started it: more stretch, more hormone, stronger contractions.

distractors.text: Smooth muscle of the uterus relaxes
distractors.why: Relaxing would reduce the stretch. In this loop the uterus contracts harder.

distractors.text: The loop switches itself off as the stretch shrinks
distractors.why: That is how negative feedback ends. Here the stretch keeps growing until an outside event, the birth, removes it.

distractors.text: Temperature control center in the brain
distractors.why: Body temperature is a different variable with its own loop.

loops.classify: The response (stronger contractions, more stretch) strengthens the stimulus, so this is positive feedback. It stops only when something outside the loop ends it: delivery removes the stretch.

failure.q: Suppose the pituitary gland could not release the hormone during labor. What would happen to this loop?

options.text: This loop could no longer drive the contractions harder
options.why: Right. The stretch is still sensed and signaled, but the command that strengthens the contractions through this loop never reaches the uterus. Labor may still go on: other signals made in the uterus itself also drive contractions, and women who release little of this hormone have had normal labors. Hospitals can give the hormone as a drug when contractions are weak.

options.text: Contractions would stop at once, because the sensor fails too
options.why: The sensor is not affected. Stretch is still detected; the command is what is missing.

options.text: Contractions would grow stronger faster, because nothing limits the loop
options.why: The hormone is what strengthens the contractions in this loop. Without it, they cannot build up this way.

options.text: The loop would run as before, with the uterus as its own control center
options.why: The uterus does not take over as the control center. In this loop the command to contract harder travels as the hormone, so without it the loop cannot drive the contractions.

loops.title: Baroreceptor reflex: pressure falls
loops.map: Baroreceptor reflex: pressure falls and pressure rises
loops.scenario: You stand up quickly after lying down. Blood pools in your leg veins and your mean arterial pressure dips, but within a few heartbeats it is back near normal.

stimulus.text: Mean arterial pressure falls
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a fall in the regulated variable, mean arterial pressure.

sensor.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch stretch less and fire less
sensor.why: Baroreceptors are stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the artery wall. Lower pressure stretches the wall less, so they fire fewer action potentials.

afferent.text: Fewer impulses in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
afferent.short: Fewer impulses in nerves IX and X
afferent.why: The carotid sinuses report through the glossopharyngeal nerves and the aortic arch through the vagus nerves. Fewer impulses reach the brainstem.

control.text: Cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata
control.why: The cardiovascular center reads less input as low pressure.

efferent.text: Sympathetic output rises and vagal output falls
efferent.why: The commands leave on autonomic nerves: more sympathetic, less parasympathetic.

effector.text: SA node, ventricular muscle, and smooth muscle of arterioles and veins
effector.why: The SA node speeds up, the ventricles contract harder, arterioles constrict and veins squeeze blood toward the heart.

response.text: Heart rate, stroke volume and TPR rise, so MAP rises back toward its set point
response.short: HR, SV, TPR rise: MAP recovers
response.why: By MAP = HR × SV × TPR, pressure climbs back, which restores baroreceptor firing and removes the stimulus.

distractors.text: Vagal output rises and sympathetic output falls
distractors.why: That is the command for a rise in pressure. It would lower pressure further here.

distractors.text: The kidneys release renin
distractors.why: Renin starts a hormone loop that raises pressure over minutes to hours. The baroreceptor reflex works through nerves within seconds.

distractors.text: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
distractors.why: Osmoreceptors sense the concentration of the plasma, not arterial pressure.

loops.classify: The response (pressure rises) opposes the stimulus (pressure falls), so the baroreceptor reflex is negative feedback.

failure.q: Long-standing diabetes mellitus has damaged a patient’s autonomic nerves, so commands from the cardiovascular center barely reach the heart and vessels. What happens when this patient stands up?

options.text: Pressure stays low, and the patient feels faint
options.why: Right. The fall is sensed and the center responds, but the efferent pathway cannot deliver the commands. Heart rate and TPR do not rise, and orthostatic hypotension results.

options.text: Pressure recovers normally, because the baroreceptors still work
options.why: Sensing the fall is only the start. Without working efferent nerves, the effectors never get the command.

options.text: Pressure rises too high, because the loop has no brake
options.why: A broken efferent pathway weakens the response; it does not strengthen it.

options.text: Heart rate rises extra fast to make up for the vessels
options.why: The same damaged autonomic nerves supply the SA node, so heart rate cannot rise much either.

loops.title: Baroreceptor reflex: pressure rises
loops.map: Baroreceptor reflex: pressure falls and pressure rises
loops.scenario: You strain to lift something heavy, then relax. Your arterial pressure overshoots for a few seconds, and your heart rate drops sharply before everything settles.

stimulus.text: Mean arterial pressure rises suddenly
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a rise in mean arterial pressure.

sensor.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinuses and aortic arch stretch more and fire faster
sensor.why: Higher pressure stretches the artery wall more, and the baroreceptors fire faster.

afferent.text: More impulses in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
afferent.short: More impulses in nerves IX and X
afferent.why: More impulses travel to the brainstem.

control.text: Cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata
control.why: The cardiovascular center reads more input as high pressure.

efferent.text: Vagal output rises and sympathetic output falls
efferent.why: The commands shift toward the parasympathetic side.

effector.text: SA node, ventricular muscle, and smooth muscle of arterioles and veins
effector.why: The SA node slows, ventricular contractions weaken slightly, and arterioles and veins relax.

response.text: Heart rate, stroke volume and TPR fall, so MAP falls back toward its set point
response.short: HR, SV, TPR fall: MAP recovers
response.why: Lower heart rate, stroke volume and resistance bring pressure back down, and baroreceptor firing returns to normal.

distractors.text: Sympathetic output rises and vagal output falls
distractors.why: That command raises pressure. It is the response to a fall, not a rise.

distractors.text: Atrial muscle cells release ANP
distractors.why: ANP responds to atrial stretch from high blood volume and acts over hours through the kidneys. It is a separate loop.

distractors.text: Chemoreceptors report falling pH
distractors.why: Chemical sensors report blood chemistry. This loop is driven by stretch of the artery wall.

loops.classify: The response (pressure falls) opposes the stimulus (pressure rises), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A person’s blood pressure stays high for weeks. Their baroreceptors reset and now treat the higher pressure as normal. What does the baroreceptor reflex do about the high pressure?

options.text: It stops opposing it and defends the new, higher level instead
options.why: Right. After resetting, the sensors fire at their normal rate at the high pressure, so the control center sees nothing to correct. This is why the baroreceptor reflex handles fast changes but cannot fix a pressure that stays high for weeks.

options.text: It keeps lowering pressure until it returns to the old normal
options.why: Once the sensors reset, they no longer report the pressure as high, so the loop has no stimulus to act on.

options.text: It raises pressure further, because the reset makes it positive feedback
options.why: Resetting moves the level the loop defends. The loop still opposes changes around that level.

options.text: It stops working at all, so pressure swings wildly
options.why: The reflex still corrects sudden changes; it just centers them on the new level.

loops.title: Renin–angiotensin–aldosterone: pressure and volume fall
loops.scenario: After a day of vomiting, a patient has lost fluid and their blood pressure is low. Over the next hours their kidneys make very little urine and their pressure slowly improves.

stimulus.text: Blood pressure and blood volume fall
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the fall in blood volume and pressure, felt in the kidney’s own vessels.

sensor.text: Pressure-sensing cells in the walls of the kidney’s small arteries
sensor.why: Specialized cells in the kidney’s vessel walls respond to lower pressure (and to sympathetic signals and low salt delivery in the kidney).

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the sensing cells release the enzyme themselves
afferent.why: The sensing cells and the releasing cells are the same, so no nerve or hormone carries the information to them.

control.text: The same kidney cells set how much renin to release
control.why: These cells release more renin the lower the pressure they sense.

efferent.text: Renin leads to angiotensin II, which triggers aldosterone release; both travel in the blood
efferent.why: Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, ACE converts that to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II makes the adrenal cortex release aldosterone. The commands travel as chemical messengers in the blood.

effector.text: Arteriole smooth muscle and the kidney tubules
effector.why: Angiotensin II constricts arterioles. Aldosterone makes the kidney tubules reabsorb more sodium, and water follows.

response.text: TPR rises and the kidneys keep more sodium and water, so blood volume and pressure rise
response.short: TPR and volume rise: pressure recovers
response.why: Higher resistance raises pressure within minutes; retained sodium and water restore volume over hours to days.

distractors.text: Stretched atrial cells release ANP
distractors.why: ANP responds to high volume and makes the kidneys lose sodium, the opposite of what is needed here.

distractors.text: The kidneys excrete more sodium and water
distractors.why: Losing more sodium and water would lower volume further.

distractors.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinuses fire faster
distractors.why: Low pressure makes baroreceptors fire less, and they belong to the fast nerve-based loop.

loops.classify: The response (pressure and volume rise) opposes the stimulus (pressure and volume fall), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A patient takes an ACE inhibitor, so little angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II. They then lose blood in an accident. How does this loop respond?

options.text: Renin rises, but little angiotensin II or aldosterone follows
options.why: Right. The sensor and control center still work, so renin release rises. The broken step in the efferent pathway means the vasoconstriction and sodium retention it would trigger are much smaller.

options.text: The loop responds normally, because renin still rises
options.why: Renin is only the first step. Its effects depend on angiotensin II being made.

options.text: Renin release stops, because the drug blocks the kidney cells
options.why: The drug blocks the converting enzyme, not the renin-releasing cells. Renin actually rises.

options.text: Aldosterone rises more than usual to make up for the missing angiotensin II
options.why: Angiotensin II is the main stimulus for aldosterone release, so aldosterone rises less, not more.

loops.title: ADH: plasma osmolarity rises
loops.scenario: After a salty meal and a long afternoon without a drink, your plasma is slightly more concentrated than usual. You feel thirsty and pass only a little dark urine.

stimulus.text: Plasma osmolarity rises
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a rise in the concentration of solutes in the plasma.

sensor.text: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
sensor.why: Osmoreceptors are sensory receptors that shrink when the fluid around them becomes more concentrated, and they fire more.

afferent.text: Signals within the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The sensors sit in the hypothalamus itself, so the afferent pathway is short: neurons within the same region.

control.text: The hypothalamus
control.why: The hypothalamus compares plasma osmolarity with its set point.

efferent.text: ADH released from the posterior pituitary into the blood
efferent.why: Hypothalamic neurons release ADH from their endings in the posterior pituitary, and it travels in the blood.

effector.text: Cells of the kidney tubules
effector.why: ADH makes the kidney tubules more permeable to water.

response.text: The tubules reabsorb more water, so less, more concentrated urine is made and plasma osmolarity falls
response.why: Water returned to the blood dilutes the plasma, opposing the rise. Thirst, driven by the same sensors, adds water by mouth.

distractors.text: The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone
distractors.why: Aldosterone makes the kidneys keep sodium. Keeping more solute would not correct concentrated plasma.

distractors.text: The kidney tubules let more water leave in the urine
distractors.why: Losing more water would make the plasma even more concentrated.

distractors.text: Stretched atrial cells release ANP
distractors.why: ANP responds to atrial stretch from high volume, not to plasma concentration.

loops.classify: The response (water kept, plasma diluted) opposes the stimulus (plasma too concentrated), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: After a head injury, the posterior pituitary releases almost no ADH (diabetes insipidus). What happens?

options.text: The kidneys make large volumes of dilute urine, and plasma osmolarity rises unless the person drinks a lot
options.why: Right. The rise in osmolarity is sensed, but no ADH reaches the tubules, so they cannot hold water back. Thirst still works, so drinking can keep up if water is available.

options.text: Urine becomes very concentrated, because the kidneys sense the high osmolarity themselves
options.why: The tubules keep water only when ADH tells them to. Without it, urine stays dilute.

options.text: Nothing changes, because aldosterone takes over the job
options.why: Aldosterone controls sodium, not the water permeability of the tubules. It cannot replace ADH.

options.text: Plasma osmolarity falls, because the kidneys keep too much water
options.why: That would be the result of too much ADH. With none, water is lost.

loops.title: ANP: blood volume rises
loops.scenario: A patient receives two liters of isotonic saline by IV over half an hour. Over the next hours they pass much more urine than usual, and their blood volume returns toward normal.

stimulus.text: Blood volume rises
stimulus.why: The stimulus is a rise in blood volume, which raises venous return and stretches the atria.

sensor.text: Atrial muscle cells are stretched
sensor.why: Atrial muscle cells respond directly to being stretched.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the stretched cells release the hormone themselves
afferent.why: The stretched cells are also the ones that release the hormone, so nothing needs to carry the signal to them.

control.text: The same atrial muscle cells set how much ANP to release
control.why: The more they are stretched, the more ANP they release.

efferent.text: ANP carried in the blood
efferent.why: The command travels as a hormone in the blood.

effector.text: The kidneys, and the smooth muscle of arterioles
effector.why: ANP makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, relaxes arterioles and holds back renin, aldosterone and ADH.

response.text: The kidneys excrete more sodium and water, so blood volume falls back toward normal
response.short: Sodium and water lost: volume falls
response.why: Excreting sodium and water lowers blood volume, opposing the rise.

distractors.text: The kidneys release renin
distractors.why: Renin starts the loop that keeps sodium and raises volume, the opposite of what is needed here.

distractors.text: ADH release rises
distractors.why: More ADH would make the kidneys keep water and raise volume further.

distractors.text: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus
distractors.why: Isotonic fluid raises volume without changing concentration. This loop senses stretch, not osmolarity.

loops.classify: The response (volume lost in urine) opposes the stimulus (volume rises), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A patient’s kidneys are badly damaged. Their stretched atria release plenty of ANP, but the kidneys respond to it only weakly. What happens to blood volume?

options.text: It stays high, because the kidneys barely act on the ANP
options.why: Right. The sensor, control center and pathway all work, and ANP levels are high. The weak kidney response lets sodium and water, and so volume, stay high.

options.text: It falls to normal, because ANP levels are high
options.why: A high hormone level achieves nothing if the target cannot respond to it.

options.text: It falls too low, because the loop overshoots
options.why: The effector is weak, so the loop undershoots; it does not overshoot.

options.text: It stays normal, because the atrial cells stop being stretched
options.why: The atria stay stretched as long as the volume stays high. The stimulus persists.

loops.title: Carbon dioxide rises in the blood
loops.map: Blood carbon dioxide and pH (chemoreceptor loop)
loops.scenario: You hold your breath for 40 seconds. Carbon dioxide keeps arriving at your lungs but none leaves. When you let go, your first breaths are deep and fast, and within a minute your breathing settles back to normal.

stimulus.text: Arterial PCO2 rises, and hydrogen ions rise with it
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is arterial PCO2. Through CO2 + H2O ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, more carbon dioxide also means more hydrogen ions and a lower pH.

sensor.text: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata, and peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
sensor.why: Carbon dioxide crosses the blood–brain barrier and lowers the pH of the brain’s fluid, which the central chemoreceptors sense; they supply most of the response. The carotid bodies sense the rise in arterial PCO2 within seconds.

afferent.text: Short connections within the brainstem, and the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
afferent.short: Brainstem links; cranial nerves IX, X
afferent.why: The central chemoreceptors sit next to the respiratory centers, so short links within the brainstem carry their signal. The glossopharyngeal nerves carry signals from the carotid bodies and the vagus nerves from the aortic bodies.

control.text: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata and pons
control.why: These groups of neurons generate the breathing rhythm and set how deep and fast each breath is.

efferent.text: Motor neurons in the phrenic and intercostal nerves
efferent.why: The phrenic nerves (from spinal segments C3 to C5) carry the command to the diaphragm, and the intercostal nerves to the intercostal muscles.

effector.text: The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles
effector.why: These breathing muscles contract harder and more often, enlarging the thorax more with each breath.

response.text: Deeper, faster breathing raises alveolar ventilation, more carbon dioxide is breathed out, and arterial PCO2 and pH return toward normal
response.why: At a steady carbon dioxide production, arterial PCO2 is inversely proportional to alveolar ventilation, so more ventilation lowers it and removes the stimulus.

distractors.text: Central chemoreceptors detect a fall in blood oxygen
distractors.why: Central chemoreceptors respond to hydrogen ions in the brain’s fluid, not to oxygen. Only the peripheral chemoreceptors make you breathe more when oxygen is low.

distractors.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus
distractors.why: Baroreceptors sit next to the carotid bodies but sense stretch from blood pressure. They report to the cardiovascular center, not the respiratory centers.

distractors.text: Breathing becomes slower and shallower
distractors.why: Less ventilation would let carbon dioxide build up further, pushing the variable away from its set point.

distractors.text: The kidneys excrete more acid over the next few days
distractors.why: The kidneys do adjust pH, but over days. This loop corrects PCO2 within minutes, by breathing.

loops.classify: The response (more carbon dioxide breathed out) opposes the stimulus (carbon dioxide rising), so this is negative feedback. As PCO2 falls back, chemoreceptor firing and breathing ease off.

failure.q: A diving accident injures the spinal cord at the level of the second cervical vertebra, cutting the pathway from the brainstem to the motor neurons of the phrenic nerves. The chemoreceptors and respiratory centers still work. What happens to arterial PCO2 without a ventilator?

options.text: It climbs, because the command cannot reach the diaphragm
options.why: Right. The chemoreceptors fire hard and the respiratory centers send their command, but the injury lies above the C3 to C5 segments that give rise to the phrenic nerves, so the diaphragm never gets it. With no ventilation, carbon dioxide builds up.

options.text: It stays normal, because the chemoreceptors still sense it
options.why: Sensing is only the first step. If the command cannot reach the muscles, detecting the rise changes nothing.

options.text: It falls, because the respiratory centers fire harder
options.why: Firing harder only helps if the signal reaches the muscles. Here it is blocked below the brainstem.

options.text: It stays normal, because the diaphragm contracts on its own rhythm
options.why: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle. It contracts only when its motor neurons fire; the rhythm comes from the brainstem.

loops.title: Oxygen falls in the arterial blood
loops.scenario: A hiker drives from the coast to a pass at 4,000 m. Within minutes of arriving, her arterial PO2 has fallen below 60 mm Hg, and she notices she is breathing more deeply even while sitting still.

stimulus.text: Arterial PO2 falls, strongly below about 60 mm Hg
stimulus.why: The variable is the partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood. The carotid bodies’ firing rises only a little as PO2 falls from 100 to about 60 mm Hg, then steeply below that, so this loop matters most below 60.

sensor.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors, mainly the carotid bodies
sensor.why: The carotid bodies, at the fork of each common carotid artery, are the only sensors that make you breathe more when oxygen is low. The aortic bodies play a small part in adults.

afferent.text: The glossopharyngeal nerves
afferent.why: Signals from the carotid bodies travel to the medulla oblongata in the glossopharyngeal nerves; the few from the aortic bodies travel in the vagus nerves.

control.text: The respiratory centers in the brainstem
control.why: The dorsal respiratory group receives the chemoreceptor input, and the medullary and pontine groups raise the depth and rate of breathing.

efferent.text: The phrenic and intercostal nerves
efferent.why: These carry the stronger, more frequent commands from the brainstem and spinal cord to the breathing muscles.

effector.text: The diaphragm and intercostal muscles
effector.why: They contract harder and more often, moving more air in and out each minute.

response.text: More ventilation raises alveolar PO2, and with it arterial PO2
response.why: More fresh air reaching the alveoli raises alveolar PO2, so more oxygen diffuses into the blood and the stimulus shrinks.

distractors.text: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla oblongata
distractors.why: The central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen at all. At altitude they even act as a brake, because the extra breathing lowers carbon dioxide.

distractors.text: Sensors that measure how much oxygen the blood carries
distractors.why: The carotid bodies sense the partial pressure of oxygen, not the amount carried. That is why anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, with a normal PO2, barely raises breathing.

distractors.text: The kidneys release erythropoietin
distractors.why: Erythropoietin does rise at altitude, but it acts over weeks, through the bone marrow. This loop answers within seconds, through breathing.

loops.classify: The response (more oxygen reaching the blood) opposes the stimulus (oxygen falling), so this is negative feedback. As arterial PO2 recovers, carotid body firing falls again.

failure.q: A man had both carotid bodies removed during neck surgery years ago. He takes a cable car to 4,000 m, and his arterial PO2 falls to 50 mm Hg. How does his breathing respond, compared with someone whose carotid bodies are intact?

options.text: It barely rises, because nothing now senses the low oxygen
options.why: Right. The carotid bodies are the only sensors that drive breathing up when oxygen falls. Without them, his central chemoreceptors still respond to carbon dioxide, but nothing reports the low PO2.

options.text: It rises normally, because the central chemoreceptors take over
options.why: The central chemoreceptors sense hydrogen ions made from carbon dioxide, not oxygen. They cannot stand in for the carotid bodies here.

options.text: It rises more than normal, because the brake from carbon dioxide is gone
options.why: The carbon dioxide brake appears only when breathing rises. Without the oxygen sensors, breathing does not rise in the first place.

options.text: It stops, because the respiratory rhythm comes from the carotid bodies
options.why: The rhythm is generated in the medulla oblongata. He breathes normally at sea level; only the response to low oxygen is lost.

loops.title: The lungs inflate a lot (Hering–Breuer reflex)
loops.scenario: During a hard run, each breath grows to about three times its resting size. As the lungs fill, each breath in is cut short a little earlier, which limits how far they are stretched.

stimulus.text: The lungs inflate far more than in a resting breath
stimulus.why: The variable is how far the lungs are stretched. At rest the reflex is weak; it becomes active at breaths about three times resting size or more.

sensor.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the smooth muscle of the airways
sensor.why: These sensory receptors fire faster as the airways and lungs are stretched by inflation.

afferent.text: The vagus nerves
afferent.why: Signals from the lung stretch sensors travel up the vagus nerves to the medulla oblongata.

control.text: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata
control.why: The stretch signals inhibit the neurons that drive inspiration, switching the breath in off sooner.

efferent.text: Fewer signals in the phrenic nerves
efferent.why: Once inspiration is switched off, the burst of signals down the phrenic nerves stops.

effector.text: The diaphragm
effector.why: The diaphragm, the main muscle of inspiration, stops contracting when its commands stop.

response.text: The breath in ends sooner, and further inflation is limited
response.why: Ending inspiration earlier stops the lungs from stretching further, opposing the stimulus.

distractors.text: Irritant sensory receptors in the airway lining detect dust and smoke
distractors.why: Irritant sensory receptors cause coughing and bronchoconstriction. They respond to particles and fumes, not to inflation.

distractors.text: The glossopharyngeal nerves
distractors.why: The glossopharyngeal nerves carry signals from the carotid bodies. Lung stretch signals travel in the vagus nerves.

distractors.text: The diaphragm contracts harder to fill the lungs further
distractors.why: That would stretch the lungs more, pushing the variable further from where the reflex holds it.

loops.classify: The response (the breath in stops) opposes the stimulus (the lungs stretching further), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A patient’s vagus nerves are blocked on both sides by a local anesthetic. What happens to his breathing?

options.text: Little changes at rest; only very large breaths run on
options.why: Right. In adults at rest the reflex is weak, so quiet breathing barely changes. Its job is limiting very large breaths, and without the vagus nerves the stretch signals cannot reach the medulla.

options.text: He stops breathing, because the vagus nerves carry the rhythm
options.why: The rhythm comes from neurons in the medulla oblongata. The vagus nerves carry sensory information to them, not the rhythm itself.

options.text: His diaphragm is paralyzed
options.why: The diaphragm is driven by the phrenic nerves, which are untouched.

options.text: His breaths become very small
options.why: Losing a signal that ends inspiration cannot make breaths smaller. If anything, large breaths go on longer.

loops.title: Your calf muscles are stretched as you tip forward
loops.scenario: You are standing on a bus when it brakes hard. Your body tips forward, which stretches your calf muscles. A split second later, before you have decided anything, they contract and help pull you back upright.

stimulus.text: The calf muscles are stretched as you tip forward
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is muscle length. Tipping forward lengthens the gastrocnemius and soleus beyond their length a moment before.

sensor.text: Muscle spindles in the calf muscles
sensor.why: Spindles lie parallel to the ordinary muscle fibers, so they are stretched with the muscle. Stretch opens mechanically gated channels in their sensory endings, and the faster and farther the stretch, the faster they fire.

afferent.text: Spindle sensory neurons entering the cord through the dorsal roots
afferent.why: The spindle’s sensory neuron has its cell body in a dorsal root ganglion and carries the signal into the sacral cord.

control.text: A single synapse on lower motor neurons in the ventral horn
control.why: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic. The integration center is the synapse where the sensory axon releases glutamate directly onto the motor neurons of the same muscle.

efferent.text: Lower motor neurons leaving through the ventral roots and the tibial nerve
efferent.why: The lower motor neuron is the final common path to skeletal muscle: its axon leaves in the ventral root and reaches the calf in the tibial nerve.

effector.text: The gastrocnemius and soleus
effector.why: The stretched muscle itself is the effector: acetylcholine at its neuromuscular junctions makes its fibers contract.

response.text: The calf muscles contract and shorten, pulling you back upright
response.why: Contraction shortens the muscle back toward its earlier length, which removes the stretch that started the loop.

distractors.text: Golgi tendon organs in the calcaneal tendon
distractors.why: Tendon organs sit in series with the muscle and report tension, not length. Their reflex inhibits the same muscle, the opposite of what is needed here.

distractors.text: Interneurons that inhibit the calf muscles’ own motor neurons
distractors.why: In a stretch reflex the inhibitory interneurons act on the antagonist, the tibialis anterior (reciprocal inhibition), not on the stretched muscle.

distractors.text: The primary motor cortex decides to tighten the calf
distractors.why: The stretch reflex closes in the spinal cord within a few tens of milliseconds, before any decision. The larger correction that follows runs through the brainstem motor tracts, not a decision in the motor cortex.

distractors.text: The tibialis anterior contracts and lifts the toes
distractors.why: The tibialis anterior is the antagonist of the calf. The stretch reflex inhibits it, so it does not fight the correction.

loops.classify: The response (the muscle shortening) opposes the stimulus (the muscle being stretched), so this is negative feedback: it holds muscle length, and with it your posture, near where it was.

failure.q: A disease destroys the large sensory axons from the muscle spindles of the legs, but spares the motor neurons and muscles. What happens when a clinician taps the calcaneal tendon?

options.text: The ankle jerk is brisker, because the motor neurons are released from control
options.why: Brisk reflexes come from losing descending control, which is upper motor neuron damage. Here the loop has lost its way in.

options.text: The ankle jerk is absent, because the stretch signal never reaches the cord
options.why: Right. The spindles still sense the stretch, but without their sensory axons nothing reaches the ventral horn, so the healthy motor neurons are never told to fire.

options.text: The ankle jerk is normal, because the motor neurons and muscle are healthy
options.why: A healthy output is useless without an input. Every part of the arc must work for the reflex to appear.

options.text: The calf contracts but the foot does not move, because the tendon is loose
options.why: The tendon is not damaged. The break is in the sensory limb, so the calf never receives the command at all.

loops.title: Bright light narrows the pupils
loops.scenario: You step out of a dark building into bright sunshine. Within about a second both pupils narrow, and the light reaching your retinas falls back toward a comfortable level.

stimulus.text: More light strikes the retina
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the amount of light reaching the retina, which rose when you stepped into the sun.

sensor.text: Photoreceptors and light-sensitive ganglion cells in the retina
sensor.why: Rods and cones, and a small set of retinal ganglion cells that respond to light themselves, detect the increase.

afferent.text: Ganglion cell axons in the optic nerve and optic tract, leaving before the thalamus
afferent.why: The signal travels in the optic nerve, then peels off the optic tract before the lateral geniculate nucleus, toward the midbrain.

control.text: The pretectal area of the midbrain, which signals the oculomotor parasympathetic nuclei on both sides
control.why: The pretectal area integrates the signal and sends it to both sides, which is why the unlit pupil narrows too.

efferent.text: Parasympathetic fibers in both oculomotor nerves, relaying in a ganglion behind each eye
efferent.why: The command travels in the parasympathetic axons of each oculomotor nerve, with a relay in the small ganglion behind the eye.

effector.text: The circular sphincter muscle of each iris
effector.why: The ring of smooth muscle around each pupil contracts, making the opening smaller.

response.text: Both pupils narrow (miosis), so less light reaches each retina
response.why: A smaller opening lets less light in, pushing the variable back toward its earlier level.

distractors.text: The radial dilator fibers of the iris contract
distractors.why: The dilator fibers widen the pupil. They are driven by sympathetic fibers, whose output falls in bright light.

distractors.text: The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus
distractors.why: That is the relay for seeing, on the way to the visual cortex. The pupil reflex leaves the pathway before the thalamus.

distractors.text: The ciliary muscle contracts and the lens rounds up
distractors.why: That is accommodation, part of the near response to a close object, not the response to bright light.

distractors.text: Sympathetic fibers in the facial nerve
distractors.why: The pupil’s narrowing is parasympathetic, and those fibers travel in the oculomotor nerve, not the facial nerve.

loops.classify: The response (less light entering) opposes the stimulus (more light striking the retina), so this is negative feedback. In dim light the loop runs the other way and the pupils widen.

failure.q: After a head injury, rising pressure squeezes the right oculomotor nerve. The optic nerves are healthy. A light is shone into the right eye. What do the pupils do?

options.text: Neither pupil narrows, because the light signal cannot get in
options.why: The light signal enters through the right optic nerve, which is healthy. This is an efferent problem, not an afferent one.

options.text: Both pupils narrow normally
options.why: The right pupil’s command travels in the squeezed nerve, so it cannot narrow.

options.text: The left pupil narrows, but the right stays wide
options.why: Right. The signal gets in and the midbrain sends commands to both sides, but only the left oculomotor nerve can carry its command. A wide, unresponsive pupil after a head injury is an emergency sign.

options.text: The right pupil narrows, but the left stays wide
options.why: The left oculomotor nerve is healthy and still receives the midbrain’s command, so the left pupil narrows. It is the right one that cannot.

loops.title: Blood pressure dips as you stand up
loops.scenario: You stand up quickly after lying on a couch. Blood pools in the veins of your legs, less returns to your heart, and the pressure in your large arteries dips. Within a few heartbeats it is back to normal.

stimulus.text: Pressure in the large arteries falls
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the blood pressure in the large arteries. Standing lets blood pool in the legs, so less is pumped out and the pressure dips.

sensor.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the walls of the large arteries near the heart and in the neck
sensor.why: These sensory receptors fire in proportion to how far the artery wall is stretched. Lower pressure stretches it less, so they fire less.

afferent.text: Visceral sensory neurons in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves
afferent.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve carries signals from the sensors in the neck and the vagus nerve from those near the heart.

control.text: Autonomic centers in the medulla oblongata
control.why: The brainstem holds the main autonomic reflex centers. They compare the input with the usual level and reset autonomic output.

efferent.text: Less vagal output, and more sympathetic output through the cardiac accelerator and vasomotor nerves
efferent.why: The two divisions change in opposite directions: vagal tone on the heart falls while sympathetic tone to the heart and vessels rises.

effector.text: The heart’s pacemaker and muscle, and the smooth muscle of small arteries and veins
effector.why: Beta-1 receptor proteins speed and strengthen the heart; alpha-1 receptor proteins constrict the vessels.

response.text: The heart beats faster and harder and the vessels constrict, so arterial pressure rises back toward normal
response.why: More blood pumped into narrower vessels raises the pressure, which restores the stretch on the artery walls and removes the stimulus.

distractors.text: Parasympathetic fibers constrict the small arteries
distractors.why: Most blood vessels have no parasympathetic fibers. They are controlled by changing sympathetic tone alone.

distractors.text: Vagal output rises to slow the heart
distractors.why: That is the response to a rise in pressure. Here pressure has fallen, so vagal output falls.

distractors.text: Warm neurons in the hypothalamus drive sweating
distractors.why: That belongs to temperature control. This loop is run by the medulla oblongata, from the stretch of the artery walls.

distractors.text: The primary motor cortex tightens the leg muscles
distractors.why: The correction is automatic and autonomic. It works in someone who is not paying attention, within a few heartbeats.

loops.classify: The response (pressure rising) opposes the stimulus (pressure falling), so this is negative feedback, carried entirely by changes in autonomic tone. A rise in pressure runs the same loop the other way.

failure.q: A man takes a drug that blocks alpha-1 receptor proteins, then stands up quickly. The sensory receptors, nerves and medulla oblongata all work normally. What happens?

options.text: The heart rate fails to rise, because the reflex is blocked
options.why: The heart works through beta-1 and muscarinic receptor proteins, which the drug does not touch, so the heart rate rises.

options.text: Pressure does not fall at all, because the sensors still detect the change
options.why: Detecting a fall does not prevent it. The correction depends on the effectors responding.

options.text: Pressure recovers fully, because the heart makes up the difference
options.why: The heart speeds up, but without vessel constriction it cannot fully restore the pressure, especially on standing.

options.text: The heart speeds up, but pressure stays low for longer
options.why: Right. The medulla sends more sympathetic output everywhere, but NE cannot constrict vessels through blocked alpha-1 receptor proteins. Only the heart responds, so the pressure stays low for longer.

loops.title: Erythropoietin restores oxygen delivery
loops.scenario: You donate a unit of blood. Your plasma volume is back within a day or two, but your red cells take weeks to catch up. Build the loop that brings them back.

stimulus.text: Diluted blood delivers less oxygen to the kidney tissue
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is oxygen delivery, not the number of red cells. After a donation, refilled plasma dilutes the remaining red cells, so each liter of blood carries less oxygen to the kidneys.

sensor.text: Oxygen-sensing cells in the kidney tissue, between the tiny tubes
sensor.why: These cells are the sensory receptors of the loop. In low oxygen, a transcription factor that is normally destroyed within minutes survives inside them.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the surviving factor switches on the EPO gene in the same cells
afferent.why: The information never leaves the cell that sensed it. No nerve or messenger carries it; the transcription factor acts on the gene directly.

control.text: The same kidney cells set how much EPO to release
control.why: The lower the oxygen they sense, the more EPO they make. They compare the oxygen reaching them with what is normal for them.

efferent.text: EPO, a hormone, carried in the blood to the red bone marrow
efferent.why: The command travels as a hormone to a distant target, the marrow. A little EPO also comes from the liver.

effector.text: Erythroid precursors in the red bone marrow
effector.why: EPO binds receptor proteins on these cells, so more of them survive, divide and mature into red cells.

response.text: Reticulocytes pour out within 3–5 days, and over weeks the red cell count and oxygen delivery recover
response.short: More red cells: oxygen delivery recovers
response.why: More red cells carry more oxygen to the kidneys, which removes the stimulus, and EPO release falls back to its resting rate.

distractors.text: Bone marrow cells sense the low oxygen and speed up on their own
distractors.why: The marrow is the effector. It responds to EPO; without EPO, as in kidney failure, it does not speed up even when oxygen delivery is low.

distractors.text: Oxygen sensors in the neck signal the brain, which sends nerve signals to the marrow
distractors.why: No nerve controls red cell production. The sensor, control center and signal are all in the kidney cells and their hormone.

distractors.text: The kidney cells release more EPO as the red cell count rises
distractors.why: That would push the count ever higher. EPO release falls as oxygen delivery recovers, which is what makes this loop negative.

distractors.text: Macrophages destroy old red cells more slowly
distractors.why: Red cell lifespan stays about 120 days. The loop acts on production, not destruction.

loops.classify: The response (more red cells, more oxygen delivered) removes the stimulus (too little oxygen reaching the kidneys), so this is negative feedback. As oxygen delivery recovers, the kidney cells release less EPO and production slows to its resting rate.

failure.q: The same donor has no iron left in her stores. Her kidneys sense the low oxygen and release plenty of EPO. What happens over the next few weeks?

options.text: EPO stays high while few, small, pale red cells are made
options.why: Right. The sensor, control center and hormone all work, but the effector lacks iron for heme. Erythroblasts keep dividing without filling with hemoglobin, so the count recovers slowly and the cells are small and pale. Because oxygen delivery stays low, the stimulus persists and EPO stays high.

options.text: EPO falls, because the kidneys sense that iron is missing
options.why: The kidney cells sense oxygen, not iron. Oxygen delivery is still low, so they keep releasing EPO.

options.text: The red cell count recovers normally, because EPO is high and the marrow is healthy
options.why: EPO tells precursors to survive and divide, but each red cell needs iron for the heme in its hemoglobin. Without iron the marrow cannot build normal cells, however much EPO arrives.

options.text: The marrow makes large red cells to make up for the missing iron
options.why: Large cells come from missing B12 or folate, which stalls DNA synthesis. Missing iron gives small, pale cells.

loops.title: Thrombin makes more thrombin
loops.scenario: You cut your finger on a kitchen knife. Within a couple of minutes the bleeding slows and a firm clot seals the cut. The clotting runs as a local loop at the injury, with no nerve or brain involved.

stimulus.text: A first trickle of thrombin forms at the tear
stimulus.why: The tear brings plasma into contact with tissue factor at the same moment platelets start to stick. Tissue factor with VIIa makes a little thrombin: too little to clot, but enough to set off the loop.

sensor.text: Receptor proteins for thrombin on platelets stuck at the tear
sensor.why: Thrombin is a strong platelet activator. The platelets already stuck in the plug detect it by binding it to receptor proteins on their surface.

afferent.text: Signals inside each platelet relay the binding
afferent.why: In this local loop, no nerve or hormone carries the information. Binding sets off signals inside the platelet itself.

control.text: The platelet switches into its activated state
control.why: Activation is the switch point: the platelet swells, grows spiky projections and changes what it releases and displays.

efferent.text: Released ADP and thromboxane A2, and negatively charged phospholipid flipped to the platelet’s outer face
efferent.why: These are the outputs. ADP and thromboxane A2 reach passing platelets; the exposed phospholipid, with calcium, gives clotting factors a surface to work on.

effector.text: More platelets, and clotting factors gathered on the activated platelet surface
effector.short: Platelets and factors on their surface
effector.why: Passing platelets are activated in turn, and on the platelet surface IXa pairs with VIIIa and Xa pairs with Va. Thrombin has already activated V, VIII and XI.

response.text: A burst of thrombin, which activates still more platelets and factors
response.why: The burst converts fibrinogen to fibrin, and the new thrombin binds more platelets and activates more V, VIII and XI. More thrombin makes more thrombin.

distractors.text: Antithrombin inactivates thrombin and factor Xa
distractors.why: Antithrombin is a brake that keeps the clot from spreading beyond the injury. It limits the loop; it is not one of its parts.

distractors.text: Plasmin cuts fibrin into fragments
distractors.why: Plasmin removes the clot days later, after the wall is repaired. That is fibrinolysis, not clot building.

distractors.text: The brain sends nerve signals that tell platelets to stick
distractors.why: Clotting is a local loop. Local nerve reflexes help the vessel constrict, but no brain command controls platelets or clotting factors.

distractors.text: Healthy lining cells release nitric oxide and prostacyclin
distractors.why: These keep platelets quiet next to the injury. They confine the loop to the tear rather than driving it.

loops.classify: The response (more thrombin, more activated platelets) strengthens the stimulus that produced it, so this is positive feedback. It stops when the hole is sealed, and it stays local because flow dilutes activated factors, the healthy lining on either side keeps platelets quiet and binds thrombin, and antithrombin inactivates thrombin and Xa.

failure.q: In hemophilia A, factor VIII is missing, so IXa has no partner on the platelet surface. What happens when a boy with hemophilia A cuts his hand?

options.text: A plug and a trickle of thrombin form, but no burst: bleeding restarts
options.why: Right. Adhesion and the start of clotting on tissue factor do not need VIII. The effector step that makes the burst does, so too little fibrin forms and the soft plug gives way.

options.text: Platelets cannot stick to the cut, so no plug forms
options.why: Platelet adhesion uses von Willebrand factor and collagen, not factor VIII. Platelet problems cause skin bleeding; hemophilia causes deep, repeated bleeding.

options.text: Clotting spreads through the whole circulation, because nothing limits the loop
options.why: Missing a factor weakens the loop. The brakes (flow, healthy lining, antithrombin) are all still working.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the tissue factor–VIIa pair keeps making thrombin on its own
options.why: That pair is switched off by an inhibitor within seconds. After that, X is activated mainly by IXa with VIIIa on platelets, which is why people with hemophilia bleed.

loops.title: Blood glucose rises: insulin
loops.map: Blood glucose: glucose high and glucose low
loops.scenario: You eat a bowl of rice. Forty-five minutes later your blood glucose has climbed from about 88 to about 135 mg/dL. By two hours it is back below 100.

stimulus.text: Blood glucose rises after a meal
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the glucose concentration of the plasma. Glucose absorbed from the meal pushes it above its fasting level.

sensor.text: Beta cells of the pancreatic islets: more glucose enters, their ATP rises and their potassium channels close
sensor.why: A beta cell is its own sensor. Glucose enters by facilitated diffusion, its breakdown raises ATP, and ATP closes ATP-sensitive potassium channels, so the cell depolarizes.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the sensing cells are the releasing cells
afferent.why: Sensor and control center are the same beta cells, so no nerve or hormone carries the information between them.

control.text: The same beta cells set how much insulin to release
control.why: Depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, and the calcium that enters triggers exocytosis of insulin: the more glucose, the more insulin.

efferent.text: Insulin carried in the blood
efferent.why: Insulin leaves through the islet’s capillaries and reaches its targets in the blood. The command is a hormone, not a nerve signal.

effector.text: Liver, skeletal muscle and adipose tissue
effector.why: These cells carry insulin’s receptor protein. Muscle and fat move GLUT4 carriers to their membranes; the liver switches on glycogenesis and switches off glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

response.text: Glucose moves into cells and into storage, so blood glucose falls back to its fasting level
response.why: Glucose leaves the plasma for muscle, fat and liver, opposing the rise. As it falls, beta cell ATP falls, the potassium channels reopen and insulin release drops.

distractors.text: Alpha cells release glucagon
distractors.why: Glucagon raises blood glucose. After a meal, high glucose and insulin hold the alpha cells back.

distractors.text: Sensory nerves carry the glucose level to the hypothalamus
distractors.why: The beta cells sense glucose themselves. The loop needs no nerve at all.

distractors.text: The brain takes up more glucose because insulin moves its carriers
distractors.why: Neurons take in glucose through carriers that are always in the membrane, so their uptake does not depend on insulin.

distractors.text: The liver breaks glycogen down and releases glucose
distractors.why: That would push glucose higher. Insulin switches glycogenolysis off.

loops.classify: The response (glucose leaves the blood) opposes the stimulus (a rise in blood glucose), and the fall removes the signal that drove insulin release, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: In early type 2 diabetes, muscle, fat and liver cells respond less to a normal amount of insulin. What happens after a meal?

options.text: Beta cells release more insulin, and glucose stays near normal at first
options.why: Right. The sensor and control center still work: glucose stays higher for longer, so the beta cells release more insulin, which partly overcomes the resistance. Glucose rises only once the beta cells cannot keep up.

options.text: Insulin release stops, because the resistant cells no longer need any insulin
options.why: The beta cells respond to glucose, not to how well the targets respond. Resistance leaves glucose higher, which drives more insulin, not less.

options.text: Glucose falls too low, because the extra insulin overshoots
options.why: The extra insulin only makes up for weaker responses. The effectors respond less, so glucose does not overshoot.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the brain takes over glucose control
options.why: The brain is not part of this loop, and only insulin lowers blood glucose.

loops.title: Blood glucose falls: glucagon
loops.map: Blood glucose: glucose high and glucose low
loops.scenario: You skip breakfast. By mid-morning, some fifteen hours after dinner, your brain has been taking about 5 grams of glucose an hour out of your blood, yet your blood glucose stays near 80 mg/dL.

stimulus.text: Blood glucose falls between meals
stimulus.why: Glucose keeps leaving the plasma for the brain and other tissues, pushing the level down toward the bottom of its range.

sensor.text: Alpha cells of the pancreatic islets, helped by glucose-sensing neurons in the hypothalamus
sensor.why: Alpha cells respond directly to low glucose, and less insulin from the beta cells next door takes the brake off them.

afferent.text: No separate pathway for the alpha cells: they sense and respond themselves
afferent.why: As in the insulin arm, the islet cells are both sensor and control center, so the loop needs no nerve.

control.text: The same alpha cells set how much glucagon to release
control.why: The lower the glucose, the more glucagon the alpha cells release.

efferent.text: Glucagon carried in the blood
efferent.why: Glucagon, a water-soluble peptide, travels in the blood to its main target.

effector.text: Liver cells
effector.why: Glucagon binds G protein–coupled receptor proteins on liver cells. Skeletal muscle has almost none, so its glycogen stays in the muscle.

response.text: The liver breaks down glycogen and makes new glucose, releasing it into the blood, so glucose rises back
response.why: cAMP and protein kinase A switch on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and switch off glycogenesis. Glucose pours out of the liver and opposes the fall.

distractors.text: Skeletal muscle breaks down its glycogen and releases glucose into the blood
distractors.why: A muscle cell lacks the enzyme that frees glucose to leave it, and muscle has almost no glucagon receptor proteins, so muscle glycogen fuels only that muscle.

distractors.text: Beta cells release more insulin
distractors.why: Insulin lowers glucose. As glucose falls, beta cells cut insulin release first, at about 80 mg/dL.

distractors.text: Muscle and fat move GLUT4 carriers into their membranes
distractors.why: That is insulin’s effect, and it would pull more glucose out of the blood.

loops.classify: The response (the liver releases glucose) opposes the stimulus (a fall in blood glucose), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A person has fasted for two days, and their liver glycogen is used up. The alpha cells still release glucagon. How does the liver keep answering it?

options.text: By making new glucose from amino acids, glycerol and lactate
options.why: Right. Liver glycogen runs low within about a day, and from then on gluconeogenesis, also switched on by glucagon, supplies most of the glucose.

options.text: It cannot: blood glucose falls steadily until the person eats
options.why: Glucagon drives two processes. With glycogen gone, gluconeogenesis keeps glucose up, so the level holds.

options.text: By releasing glucose from the muscles’ glycogen store
options.why: Muscle glycogen cannot leave the muscle cell as glucose.

options.text: By making glycogen faster
options.why: Glycogenesis stores glucose; glucagon switches it off.

loops.title: Thyroid hormone falls: the thyroid axis
loops.scenario: For months, a woman eats food that is low in iodine. Her free T4 drifts down, a blood test shows a raised TSH, and TSH drives her follicular cells to trap iodide harder. Her free T4 creeps back toward normal.

stimulus.text: Free T4 and T3 in the blood fall
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the level of free thyroid hormone in the blood.

sensor.text: Cells of the anterior pituitary and neurons of the hypothalamus that respond to thyroid hormone
sensor.why: Thyroid hormone enters these cells and holds back TRH and TSH release. When less arrives, the brake weakens. The pituitary is the main site.

afferent.text: The level of thyroid hormone itself, carried to them in the blood
afferent.why: The information travels as the hormone level in the blood reaching the brain and pituitary. No nerve reports it.

control.text: The hypothalamus (TRH) and the anterior pituitary (TSH)
control.why: TRH travels through the hypophyseal portal system and drives the anterior pituitary, which sets how much TSH to release.

efferent.text: TSH carried in the blood to the thyroid gland
efferent.why: TSH is the tropic hormone that carries the command to the target gland.

effector.text: Follicular cells of the thyroid gland
effector.why: TSH binds receptor proteins on the follicular cells and, through cAMP, speeds iodide trapping, thyroglobulin making, iodination and the endocytosis of thyroid colloid.

response.text: More T4 and T3 are released, so their level rises back
response.why: The follicular cells free T4 and T3 from thyroglobulin and release them into the capillaries, opposing the fall.

distractors.text: Parafollicular cells release calcitonin
distractors.why: Calcitonin comes from the C cells and acts on calcium, not on thyroid hormone.

distractors.text: The posterior pituitary releases TSH
distractors.why: TSH comes from the anterior pituitary. The posterior lobe releases only ADH and oxytocin.

distractors.text: Thyroid hormone switches off TSH release
distractors.why: That is what happens when thyroid hormone is high. Here it is low, so TSH rises.

loops.classify: The response (more T4 and T3) opposes the stimulus (low T4 and T3), and the rising hormone then brakes TRH and TSH again, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A pituitary tumor destroys the TSH-making cells. What pattern of hormones do you expect?

options.text: Low TSH and low T4
options.why: Right. With no TSH, the follicular cells are no longer driven, so T4 falls too. Both low points to the pituitary or hypothalamus.

options.text: Low TSH and high T4
options.why: That is the pattern of a gland overproducing on its own, as in Graves disease, where feedback drives TSH down.

options.text: High TSH and low T4
options.why: That is the pattern when the thyroid gland itself fails: feedback is lost and the healthy pituitary releases more TSH.

options.text: Normal T4, because the thyroid gland works on its own
options.why: The follicular cells need TSH to keep releasing hormone and to keep their size.

loops.title: Cortisol falls: the pituitary–adrenal axis
loops.scenario: A patient taking a drug that partly blocks cortisol synthesis has a lower cortisol level for a few days. Blood tests show ACTH climbing, and cortisol creeps back toward normal.

stimulus.text: Cortisol in the blood falls
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the level of cortisol in the blood (set around a daily rhythm).

sensor.text: Neurons of the hypothalamus and cells of the anterior pituitary that respond to cortisol
sensor.why: Cortisol normally holds back CRH and ACTH release. When less of it arrives, these cells release more.

afferent.text: The cortisol level itself, carried to them in the blood
afferent.why: The information travels as the hormone level reaching the brain and pituitary, not as a nerve signal.

control.text: The hypothalamus (CRH) and the anterior pituitary (ACTH)
control.why: CRH travels through the hypophyseal portal system and makes the anterior pituitary release ACTH.

efferent.text: ACTH carried in the blood to the adrenal glands
efferent.why: ACTH is the tropic hormone that carries the command to the adrenal cortex.

effector.text: Cells of the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex
effector.why: ACTH binds receptor proteins on zona fasciculata cells, which make and release cortisol within minutes.

response.text: More cortisol is made and released, so its level rises back
response.why: Cortisol is made on demand and diffuses out, opposing the fall. As it rises, it brakes CRH and ACTH again.

distractors.text: The zona glomerulosa releases more aldosterone
distractors.why: Aldosterone answers mainly to angiotensin II and potassium, and it does not feed back on this axis.

distractors.text: Sympathetic fibers make the adrenal medulla release epinephrine
distractors.why: That is the fast, neural stress response, not the hormonal loop that holds cortisol steady.

distractors.text: The adrenal cortex releases stored cortisol from vesicles
distractors.why: Steroids are not stored. The cortex makes cortisol as it is needed and it diffuses straight out.

loops.classify: The response (cortisol rises) opposes the stimulus (cortisol falls), and cortisol then inhibits CRH and ACTH release, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: An immune attack destroys the adrenal cortex (Addison disease). What happens to ACTH?

options.text: It rises very high, as cortisol no longer brakes the pituitary
options.why: Right. The sensor and control center are intact and keep driving ACTH up, but the destroyed effector cannot answer. The high ACTH also darkens the skin.

options.text: It falls, because the adrenal glands no longer need it
options.why: The pituitary responds to the low cortisol it senses, not to whether the adrenal glands can respond.

options.text: It stays normal, because the axis is balanced
options.why: The balance depends on cortisol feeding back. With no cortisol, nothing holds ACTH down.

options.text: It falls, because aldosterone rises to take over cortisol’s feedback role
options.why: All three zones fail in Addison disease, so aldosterone falls too, and aldosterone does not control ACTH.

loops.title: Blood calcium falls: PTH and calcitriol
loops.scenario: For a week, a woman eats almost no dairy or other calcium-rich food. Her blood calcium dips slightly, then holds steady near 9 mg/dL.

stimulus.text: Blood calcium falls
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the concentration of calcium in the blood. Total calcium is held at about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL, and the free calcium ions, about half of it, are what the chief cells sense.

sensor.text: Calcium-sensing receptor proteins on the chief cells of the parathyroid glands
sensor.why: When calcium falls, fewer calcium ions bind the sensing receptor protein, and the chief cells release more hormone within seconds.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the chief cells sense and respond themselves
afferent.why: This is a humoral stimulus. The chief cells are both the sensor and the control center.

control.text: The chief cells set how much PTH to release
control.why: The lower the calcium, the more PTH the chief cells release.

efferent.text: PTH in the blood, and calcitriol that PTH has the kidneys make
efferent.why: PTH carries the command to bone and kidney, and switches on the kidney enzyme that makes calcitriol, which carries it to the intestine.

effector.text: Bone (through osteoblasts that activate osteoclasts), kidney tubules and the intestine
effector.why: PTH binds osteoblasts, which make more osteoclasts form and work; kidney tubules keep calcium and lose phosphate; calcitriol makes the intestine absorb more calcium.

response.text: Calcium is released from bone, kept by the kidneys and absorbed from food, so blood calcium rises back
response.why: All three routes add calcium to the blood, opposing the fall. As it returns to range, PTH release falls.

distractors.text: Parafollicular cells release calcitonin
distractors.why: Calcitonin is released when calcium is high, and it lowers calcium, the wrong direction here.

distractors.text: PTH binds osteoclasts directly and makes them dissolve bone
distractors.why: PTH binds osteoblasts, not osteoclasts. The osteoblasts then signal osteoclasts to form and work harder.

distractors.text: The kidneys excrete more calcium in the urine
