distractors.why: PTH makes the kidneys keep calcium. Losing more would lower calcium further.

loops.classify: The response (calcium rises) opposes the stimulus (calcium falls), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A man’s kidneys fail, so they can no longer make calcitriol, though his parathyroid glands work. What happens?

options.text: PTH rises and calcium tends to fall, because the intestine absorbs little calcium
options.why: Right. One arm of the efferent pathway is broken. Without calcitriol, the intestine absorbs little calcium, calcium dips, and the chief cells release more and more PTH to pull calcium from bone.

options.text: PTH falls, because calcitriol normally drives it
options.why: PTH drives calcitriol, not the other way round. Low calcium drives PTH up.

options.text: Calcium rises, because bone keeps releasing it
options.why: Bone helps, but without intestinal absorption the body loses its main supply, so calcium tends to fall.

options.text: Nothing changes, because calcitonin takes over
options.why: Calcitonin lowers calcium, and in adults its effect is minor. It cannot replace calcitriol.

loops.title: Blood calcium rises: less PTH (and calcitonin, minor)
loops.scenario: After a large calcium supplement and a big glass of milk, a man’s blood calcium rises a little above its set point. Within hours it is back in range.

stimulus.text: Blood calcium rises
stimulus.why: Calcium absorbed from the gut pushes the level above its set point.

sensor.text: Calcium-sensing receptor proteins on the chief cells (and the parafollicular cells of the thyroid gland)
sensor.why: More calcium binds the chief cells’ sensing receptor protein, which cuts PTH release. The C cells also sense the rise.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the gland cells sense and respond themselves
afferent.why: As with low calcium, the sensing cells are also the control center.

control.text: Chief cells cut PTH release; C cells release calcitonin
control.why: The main change is less PTH. The C cells add calcitonin, a minor extra brake in adults.

efferent.text: Less PTH in the blood, plus a little calcitonin (minor in adults)
efferent.why: With less PTH, less calcitriol is made too. Calcitonin quickly stops osteoclasts, but people without it keep normal calcium.

effector.text: Bone, kidney tubules and the intestine
effector.why: The same targets, now driven less: osteoclasts slow, the kidneys let calcium go, and with less calcitriol the intestine absorbs less.

response.text: Less calcium enters the blood and more leaves in the urine, so blood calcium falls back
response.why: The response opposes the rise and brings calcium back within about 10% of its set point.

distractors.text: Chief cells release more PTH
distractors.why: More PTH would raise calcium further. High calcium cuts PTH release.

distractors.text: The kidneys make more calcitriol
distractors.why: PTH switches the calcitriol step on, so with PTH low, less calcitriol is made.

distractors.text: Calcitonin from the parathyroid glands
distractors.why: Calcitonin comes from the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland, not the parathyroid glands.

loops.classify: The response (calcium falls) opposes the stimulus (calcium rises), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A woman’s thyroid gland, and with it all her C cells, is removed. Her parathyroid glands are unharmed. How does her calcium control change?

options.text: Hardly at all: falling PTH still does most of the work
options.why: Right. Calcitonin is a minor brake in adults. People without a thyroid gland keep normal calcium as long as their parathyroid glands work. (For your exam, calcitonin is still named as the hormone that lowers calcium.)

options.text: Calcium rises out of control, because nothing lowers it
options.why: PTH falling is the main way calcium is lowered, and that still works.

options.text: Calcium falls, because calcitonin normally raises it
options.why: Calcitonin lowers calcium; it does not raise it.

options.text: PTH stops, because the thyroid gland controls it
options.why: The chief cells sense calcium themselves; they do not need the thyroid gland.

loops.title: Plasma potassium rises: aldosterone
loops.scenario: After a large meal of bananas and potatoes, plasma potassium creeps up. Over the next hours the extra potassium leaves in the urine and the level settles.

stimulus.text: Plasma potassium rises
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the potassium concentration of the plasma. Even a small rise matters, because it changes the resting membrane potential of every cell.

sensor.text: Cells of the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex
sensor.why: Potassium acts on the glomerulosa cells directly; they are their own sensor.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: potassium acts on the releasing cells themselves
afferent.why: Like the islet cells and chief cells, these cells sense the variable and respond without a nerve.

control.text: The same glomerulosa cells set how much aldosterone to make
control.why: The higher the potassium, the more aldosterone they make and release.

efferent.text: Aldosterone carried in the blood
efferent.why: Aldosterone, a lipid-soluble steroid, travels mostly on carrier proteins to its target.

effector.text: Cells of the last stretch of the kidney’s tubules
effector.why: Aldosterone binds an intracellular receptor protein and makes the cells build more sodium channels and sodium–potassium pumps.

response.text: More potassium is secreted into the urine, so plasma potassium falls back
response.why: Potassium leaves in the urine, opposing the rise. As potassium falls, the glomerulosa cells ease off.

distractors.text: Osmoreceptors make the posterior pituitary release ADH
distractors.why: ADH answers to plasma osmolarity and makes the kidneys keep water. It does not set how much potassium they secrete.

distractors.text: ACTH from the anterior pituitary drives the zona fasciculata
distractors.why: The zona fasciculata makes cortisol. ACTH has only a small, short-lived effect on aldosterone.

distractors.text: The kidneys keep more potassium
distractors.why: Keeping potassium would push the level higher. Aldosterone makes the kidney lose it.

loops.classify: The response (potassium falls) opposes the stimulus (potassium rises), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A patient takes a drug that blocks aldosterone’s receptor protein in the kidney. What happens to plasma potassium after a potassium-rich meal?

options.text: It rises more and stays up longer
options.why: Right. The glomerulosa cells still sense the rise and release aldosterone, but the kidney cells cannot respond, so less potassium is secreted.

options.text: It falls faster, because aldosterone release rises
options.why: Aldosterone may rise, but it cannot act on a blocked receptor protein.

options.text: It stays normal, because cortisol takes aldosterone’s place in the kidney
options.why: An enzyme in those kidney cells inactivates cortisol, and the drug blocks the receptor protein anyway.

options.text: It stays normal, because potassium leaves in sweat instead
options.why: Sweat glands answer to aldosterone too, and they lose only small amounts.

loops.title: Fever: the set point is raised
loops.map: Fever: raising the temperature set point
loops.scenario: You wake with a sore throat. Macrophages fighting the infection release interleukin-1, and prostaglandin E2 in your hypothalamus raises the set point from 36.6 to 39 °C. Your hands go pale and cold, you shiver under two blankets, and over the next hour your temperature climbs to 39 °C and then holds there.

stimulus.text: Pyrogens raise the set point, so body temperature is now below it
stimulus.short: Temperature now below the set point
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the gap between the regulated variable and its set point. Your temperature has not changed; the target has moved up, which opens the same gap cold weather would.

sensor.text: Temperature-sensing nerve endings in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the hypothalamus
sensor.why: These sensory receptors report the actual temperature, exactly as they do on any day. They work normally in a fever.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carrying temperature signals to the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries information toward the control center. Signals from the skin travel on sensory nerves; the hypothalamic neurons sense blood temperature where they sit.

control.text: The hypothalamus, comparing body temperature with its raised set point
control.why: The control center compares the reading with the set point. Prostaglandin E2 has raised that set point, so a normal 36.6 °C now reads as too cold.

efferent.text: Sympathetic nerves to skin blood vessels; motor nerves to skeletal muscles
efferent.why: The efferent pathway carries commands away from the control center: sympathetic fibers to the skin arterioles and somatic motor neurons to the muscles that shiver.

effector.text: Skin arterioles (constrict) and skeletal muscles (shiver)
effector.why: The smooth muscle of skin arterioles contracts, keeping warm blood away from the surface, and skeletal muscles contract in rapid small bursts, releasing heat.

response.text: Less heat lost and more heat made, so temperature rises to the new set point and the gap closes
response.short: Temperature rises to the new set point
response.why: The response opposes the stimulus: the gap was "too cold for the set point", and warming closes it. Once temperature reaches 39 °C, the chills stop.

distractors.text: Sweat glands release sweat
distractors.why: Sweating removes heat. It runs when temperature is above the set point, as it is when the fever breaks, not while temperature is climbing toward a raised set point.

distractors.text: The hypothalamus loses control, so temperature drifts upward
distractors.why: Control is intact. Every part of the loop works normally; it is steering toward a higher target, which is why fever-reducing drugs that lower the set point work.

distractors.text: Skin arterioles dilate to carry heat to the surface
distractors.why: Dilation sheds heat. During the rising phase the arterioles constrict, which is why the skin looks pale and the hands feel cold.

distractors.text: Warm-sensitive nerve endings fire faster as the fever begins
distractors.why: At the start your temperature is still normal, so nothing warms these endings. The change is in the set point, not in what the sensors detect.

loops.classify: The response (warming) closes the gap between body temperature and the set point, so this is negative feedback, just around a higher set point. Once the gap closes, the heat-gain responses ease off, and temperature holds at the new value instead of spiraling upward as it would in positive feedback.

failure.q: A patient on a breathing machine in intensive care has been given a drug that stops his skeletal muscles from contracting. Assume his sedation leaves his temperature control unchanged. Pyrogens from an infection then raise his set point to 39 °C. What happens to his temperature?

options.text: It rises more slowly, because only the skin arterioles can respond
options.why: Right. The sensors, pathways and hypothalamus all work, and skin vasoconstriction still keeps heat in, but without shivering much less heat is made. The loop can correct only as fast as its effectors allow.

options.text: It rises just as fast, because the hypothalamus sends stronger commands
options.why: Stronger commands cannot make paralyzed muscles contract. With one effector missing, heat is gained more slowly.

options.text: It falls, because the set point drops to match what the muscles can do
options.why: The set point follows prostaglandin E2, not the state of the effectors. It stays at 39 °C while the loop falls behind.

options.text: It stays at 36.6 °C, because the fever depends entirely on shivering
options.why: Skin vasoconstriction still cuts heat loss, and the body keeps making heat by its metabolism, so temperature can still drift up, only more slowly.

loops.title: Stomach acid shuts off gastrin
loops.map: Gastric acid and gastrin (low pH shuts gastrin off)
loops.scenario: An hour into a steak dinner, the parietal cells have been secreting acid steadily. Food buffered the acid at first, but now the pH in the antrum is falling below 3, and gastrin release begins to slow.

stimulus.text: Acid builds up and the pH in the antrum falls below about 3
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the acidity of the stomach contents. Acid secreted in response to the meal outpaces the food’s buffering, and the pH drops.

sensor.text: D cells in the lining of the antrum detect the low pH
sensor.why: D cells are enteroendocrine cells that respond to acid in the lumen. They are the sensing part of this loop.

afferent.text: Somatostatin released by the D cells onto the neighboring G cells
afferent.why: The D cells pass the signal on as a local messenger. Somatostatin diffuses to the G cells beside them instead of traveling in the blood.

control.text: G cells in the antrum set how much gastrin to release
control.why: The G cells add up their inputs (protein fragments, stretch and vagal signals pushing up, somatostatin pushing down) and release gastrin accordingly.

efferent.text: Less gastrin carried in the blood
efferent.why: Gastrin leaves the antrum in the blood and reaches the body of the stomach, where the acid is made. The command is a hormone.

effector.text: ECL cells and parietal cells in the body of the stomach
effector.why: Gastrin acts mostly by making ECL cells release histamine onto the parietal cells, and partly on the parietal cells directly. With less gastrin, both are driven less.

response.text: Acid secretion slows, so the pH stops falling
response.why: Fewer hydrogen ions are pumped into the lumen, which opposes the fall in pH. When a new meal buffers the acid and the pH rises, the brake lifts again.

distractors.text: Chief cells release pepsinogen
distractors.why: Pepsinogen digests protein once it is activated. It does not measure or set the acidity.

distractors.text: Sensory neurons carry the pH to the hypothalamus
distractors.why: The pH is sensed and acted on inside the stomach wall itself. No signal goes to the brain in this loop.

distractors.text: Parietal cells pump more H+ as the pH falls
distractors.why: That would push the pH further from where it started, the opposite of what a negative feedback loop does.

distractors.text: Secretin from the small intestine
distractors.why: Secretin also slows acid secretion, but it responds to acid arriving in the small intestine. This loop is sensed in the antrum.

loops.classify: The response (less acid secreted) opposes the stimulus (a falling pH), and the product, acid, switches off its own stimulus, gastrin. That makes this negative feedback.

failure.q: In autoimmune gastritis, the immune system destroys the parietal cells but leaves the G cells and D cells in the antrum. What happens to gastrin?

options.text: Gastrin rises very high
options.why: Right. Without parietal cells no acid is made, the pH in the antrum never falls, and the D cells never release somatostatin. With the brake gone, the G cells release gastrin freely.

options.text: Gastrin falls to almost nothing, because acid-making cells are gone
options.why: The G cells are intact. Losing the parietal cells removes the acid that normally restrains them, so gastrin rises.

options.text: Gastrin is unchanged, because it is controlled by the vagus alone
options.why: Vagal signals are one input, but low pH through somatostatin is the brake. That brake is what is lost.

options.text: The D cells take over acid secretion
options.why: D cells make somatostatin, not acid. Only parietal cells make hydrochloric acid.

loops.title: A full small intestine slows the stomach
loops.scenario: After a fatty, acidic meal, chyme leaves the stomach faster than the first part of the small intestine can neutralize and digest it. Within minutes, the stomach’s waves weaken and the pylorus tightens.

stimulus.text: The first part of the small intestine fills with acid, fat and concentrated chyme
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is how much chyme the small intestine is handling at once. Chyme arriving faster than it can be processed raises the stretch, acidity and solute load there.

sensor.text: Stretch- and chemical-sensitive sensory receptors and enteroendocrine cells in the intestinal wall
sensor.why: Sensory neurons detect stretch and chemicals in the lumen, and enteroendocrine cells sense acid, fat and protein fragments.

afferent.text: Enteric and vagal sensory fibers, plus secretin and CCK in the blood
afferent.why: The signal travels two ways at once: nerve fibers carry it into the enteric plexuses and up the vagus, and the hormones carry it in the blood.

control.text: The enteric plexuses and the brainstem
control.why: Short reflexes run through the enteric plexuses; long reflexes run through the brainstem. Together they make up the enterogastric reflex.

efferent.text: Less vagal excitation and more sympathetic drive to the stomach
efferent.why: The reflex turns down the nerves that excite the stomach and turns up those that inhibit it, while the hormones act on the stomach directly.

effector.text: The smooth muscle of the antrum and the pyloric sphincter
effector.why: The antrum’s mixing waves push chyme toward the pylorus, and the sphincter decides how much passes. Changing both changes the rate of emptying.

response.text: Antral waves weaken and the pylorus tightens, so emptying slows until the intestine catches up
response.why: Less chyme enters, so the intestine has time to neutralize and digest what it has. As its load falls, the brake eases and emptying speeds up again.

distractors.text: The stomach empties faster to clear the chyme
distractors.why: That would increase the load on the overloaded intestine, the opposite of the correcting response.

distractors.text: Gastrin rises and speeds emptying
distractors.why: Gastrin mainly drives acid secretion and has little effect on emptying. The brake here comes from the intestine.

distractors.text: Motilin sweeps the intestine clear
distractors.why: Motilin drives the strong contractions between meals and is stopped by eating. It plays no part in a meal-time brake.

loops.classify: The response (slower emptying) reduces the stimulus (an overloaded small intestine), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: Suppose a drug blocked the sensory neurons and enteroendocrine cells of the first part of the small intestine. What would happen after an acidic, fatty meal?

options.text: Chyme would empty too fast for the intestine to handle
options.why: Right. With no sensing, the enterogastric reflex and the secretin and CCK brake never start, so the stomach empties as if the intestine were empty.

options.text: The stomach would stop emptying, because the pylorus would stay shut
options.why: The sensors apply the brake. Blocking them removes the brake; it does not apply it.

options.text: Nothing, because the stomach senses its own contents
options.why: The stomach sets its mixing, but the pace of emptying is set mainly by what the small intestine receives.

options.text: Acid secretion would stop
options.why: Blocking this loop removes one of the brakes on acid secretion, so acid would not fall.

loops.title: Secretin neutralizes acid in the duodenum
loops.scenario: A squirt of chyme at pH 2 enters the duodenum. Within a minute, pancreatic juice rich in bicarbonate follows it, and the duodenal contents rise back to a pH of about 6 to 7.

stimulus.text: Acid chyme lowers the pH in the duodenum
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the pH of the duodenal contents. Acid from the stomach pushes it far below the near-neutral range the pancreatic enzymes need.

sensor.text: Enteroendocrine cells in the duodenal lining detect the acid
sensor.why: These cells respond to hydrogen ions in the lumen. They are the sensors of this loop.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the sensing cells are the releasing cells
afferent.why: The cells that sense the acid are the ones that release secretin, so nothing needs to carry the signal between sensor and control center.

control.text: The same enteroendocrine cells set how much secretin to release
control.why: The more acid arrives, the more secretin these cells release.

efferent.text: Secretin carried in the blood
efferent.why: Secretin leaves through the capillaries of the duodenal wall and reaches the pancreas in the blood. The command is a hormone.

effector.text: Duct cells of the pancreas (and of the bile ducts)
effector.why: Secretin targets the duct cells, which make bicarbonate and add a large volume of watery, alkaline fluid to the pancreatic juice. Bile duct cells add some too.

response.text: Bicarbonate neutralizes the acid and the duodenal pH rises to about 6 to 7
response.why: Bicarbonate combines with hydrogen ions to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into carbon dioxide and water. With the acid gone, secretin release falls.

distractors.text: Acinar cells release trypsinogen and lipase
distractors.why: That is CCK’s main effect on the pancreas. Enzymes do not neutralize acid.

distractors.text: The gallbladder contracts
distractors.why: Gallbladder contraction is driven by CCK in response to fat, not by secretin in response to acid.

distractors.text: Parietal cells secrete more acid
distractors.why: Secretin does the opposite: it slows acid secretion by the stomach.

loops.classify: The response (acid neutralized) removes the stimulus (low duodenal pH) that released secretin, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A tumor squeezes the main pancreatic duct shut, so pancreatic juice cannot reach the duodenum. What happens to secretin and the duodenal pH after a meal?

options.text: Secretin stays high and the duodenum stays acidic
options.why: Right. The sensor and control center work, but the effector’s product cannot reach the duodenum. The acid is never removed, so the signal never switches off.

options.text: Secretin falls, because the pancreas stops responding
options.why: Secretin release depends on acid in the duodenum, not on the pancreas. The acid stays, so secretin stays high.

options.text: The duodenum is neutralized normally by bile
options.why: Bile adds a little bicarbonate, but pancreatic juice supplies most of it. The duodenum stays acidic.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the stomach stops secreting acid
options.why: Secretin slows acid secretion but does not stop it, and the stomach keeps sending acid chyme.

loops.title: Thermoregulation in full: the core is too cold
loops.scenario: A hiker waits out a storm on a windy ridge at 2 °C in damp clothes. Within minutes his skin cools, his fingers go pale, and he starts to shiver before his core temperature has fallen at all.

stimulus.text: A fall in skin temperature, and then in core temperature
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the change in the regulated variable. Cold skin gives early warning, before the core itself has cooled.

sensor.text: Cold thermoreceptors in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the hypothalamus
sensor.why: Peripheral sensory receptors report the shell; central temperature-sensitive neurons in the hypothalamus, spinal cord and abdomen report the core.

afferent.text: Sensory neurons to the spinal cord and up to the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries the skin’s signals toward the control center. Because this input arrives first, shivering can start before the core has changed.

control.text: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus, comparing the combined input with its set point
control.why: The preoptic area at the front of the hypothalamus is the control center: it weighs skin and core input against the set point and drives heat-gain responses.

efferent.text: Sympathetic nerves releasing norepinephrine to skin arterioles and brown fat; somatic motor neurons to skeletal muscle
efferent.why: Two efferent routes carry the commands: autonomic (sympathetic) fibers to smooth muscle and brown fat, and somatic motor neurons to the muscles that shiver.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of skin arterioles, skeletal muscle and brown adipose tissue
effector.why: Skin arterioles narrow; skeletal muscles contract in rapid, unsynchronized bursts; brown fat cells let H+ leak across their inner mitochondrial membranes and release heat.

response.text: Less warm blood reaches the skin and more heat is made, so core temperature is held near its set point
response.why: Narrow skin vessels turn the shell into insulation, and shivering and brown fat raise heat production. Both oppose the fall.

distractors.text: Sympathetic cholinergic nerves to the sweat glands
distractors.why: That efferent route drives sweating and active skin vasodilation, the heat-loss responses of the warm loop.

distractors.text: The thyroid gland raising heat production within minutes
distractors.why: Long cold exposure raises thyroid hormone activity a little, but in adults this is slow and minor. The fast responses come from the nervous system.

distractors.text: The set point falls to match the cold
distractors.why: The set point stays put; pyrogens move it in a fever, but cold does not. The loop works by pushing temperature back toward it.

distractors.text: Wider skin vessels to warm the fingers
distractors.why: Widening would carry core heat out to the cold surface. In the cold, skin arterioles narrow, which is why the fingers go pale.

loops.classify: The responses (less heat lost, more heat made) oppose the stimulus (cooling), so this is negative feedback. As core temperature returns toward the set point, the error signal shrinks and shivering eases off.

failure.q: The hiker has drunk several shots of alcohol, which keeps his skin vessels wide even as he chills. What happens to his core temperature on the ridge?

options.text: It falls faster than it would sober
options.why: Right. The sensors and control center still call for vasoconstriction, but the vessel effector cannot deliver it, so warm blood keeps flowing to the cold skin and heat is lost faster. Alcohol also dulls judgment, so he may not seek shelter.

options.text: It stays normal, because the warm, flushed skin feels comfortable
options.why: Feeling warm is not the same as keeping heat. Blood at the surface is losing heat to the cold air.

options.text: It rises, because the widened vessels carry more heat to the core
options.why: Widened skin vessels carry core heat outward to the surface, where it is lost; they do not bring heat in.

options.text: It falls only if the sensors are also damaged
options.why: The sensors work normally. A single weakened effector is enough to let the loop fall behind.

loops.title: Thermoregulation in full: the core is too warm
loops.scenario: A cyclist climbs a long hill on a warm afternoon. Her working muscles release heat, her skin flushes, she sweats heavily, and her core temperature rises a little and then holds steady.

stimulus.text: A rise in core temperature from the heat her muscles release
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the rise in the regulated variable: heat is being made faster than it is lost.

sensor.text: Temperature-sensitive neurons in the hypothalamus and warm thermoreceptors in the skin
sensor.why: Central temperature-sensitive neurons report the warming core, and warm thermoreceptors in the skin add input from the shell.

afferent.text: Sensory neurons from the skin to the spinal cord and up to the hypothalamus
afferent.short: Skin sensory neurons to the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries skin signals to the control center; the hypothalamic neurons sense blood temperature where they sit.

control.text: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus
control.why: The preoptic area compares the combined input with the set point, which is normal here, and drives the heat-loss responses.

efferent.text: Sympathetic cholinergic nerves to the sweat glands and skin vessels, plus less sympathetic constrictor tone
efferent.why: Sympathetic cholinergic fibers release acetylcholine onto eccrine sweat glands and cause active dilation of skin vessels in hairy skin; in the palms, soles and lips the vessels widen as constrictor tone is withdrawn.

effector.text: Eccrine sweat glands and skin blood vessels
effector.why: The sweat glands secrete sweat onto the skin, and the smooth muscle of skin vessels relaxes, so skin blood flow can rise many times over.

response.text: Sweat evaporates and warm blood reaches the skin, so more heat is lost and core temperature is held down
response.short: More heat lost: core held down
response.why: Evaporation removes about 580 kcal per liter of sweat, and blood near the surface loses heat by radiation and convection. Both oppose the rise.

distractors.text: Sympathetic nerves releasing norepinephrine onto brown fat
distractors.why: Norepinephrine to brown fat makes heat, the opposite of what a warm core needs; it belongs to the cold loop.

distractors.text: Wider blood vessels in the gut and kidneys
distractors.why: In heat stress the vessels of the gut and kidneys narrow, shifting blood toward the skin.

distractors.text: Skeletal muscles shivering
distractors.why: Shivering releases heat. It is a response to cold and would make this rise worse.

distractors.text: The set point rises, as in a fever
distractors.why: Exercise and hot weather leave the set point normal. Pyrogens raise it in a fever; here the loop works to bring temperature down to the usual target.

loops.classify: The response (more heat lost) opposes the stimulus (a rise in core temperature), so this is negative feedback. Heat loss rises until it matches the heat the muscles make, and temperature holds steady.

failure.q: An older man takes an anticholinergic drug, which blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptor proteins, and walks to the shops during a heat wave. What happens to his core temperature?

options.text: It climbs, because his sweat glands cannot respond
options.why: Right. The sensors and preoptic area work, but the sweat glands cannot respond to the acetylcholine that sympathetic cholinergic fibers release, so the main route of heat loss in hot air fails. This is one reason some drugs raise the risk of heat stroke.

options.text: It stays normal, because his skin vessels still widen
options.why: Wider skin vessels help only while the air is cooler than the skin. Once a heat wave pushes the air near or above skin temperature, evaporation is the only route left, and it is blocked.

options.text: It falls, because the drug lowers the set point
options.why: The drug acts at the sweat glands, not on the set point in the hypothalamus.

options.text: It stays normal, because shivering stops
options.why: He was not shivering. Losing a heat-gain response does nothing to make up for a heat-loss response that has failed.

loops.title: Tubuloglomerular feedback: one nephron’s GFR rises
loops.scenario: During a brisk walk, blood pressure rises for a few seconds, and filtration in one nephron starts to climb. Within seconds its own filtering settles back toward normal, with no signal from the brain.

stimulus.text: GFR in one nephron rises, so fluid rushes through its tubule
stimulus.why: Faster flow gives the tubule less time to reabsorb NaCl, so the stimulus is really a rise in NaCl delivered along the tubule.

sensor.text: Macula densa cells at the end of the thick ascending limb
sensor.why: These crowded cells in the tubule wall sense how much sodium chloride flows past them.

afferent.text: No nerve: the macula densa sits right against its own arterioles
afferent.why: The sensor and the effector belong to the same nephron and touch at the juxtaglomerular apparatus, so no nerve or hormone carries the signal a distance.

control.text: The macula densa cells set how much ATP to release
control.why: The more NaCl they take up, the more ATP they release. The same cells act as sensor and control center.

efferent.text: ATP, broken down to adenosine outside the cells
efferent.why: Adenosine is the local chemical messenger that reaches the smooth muscle next door.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole
effector.why: Adenosine acts on receptor proteins on this muscle, which contracts.

response.text: The afferent arteriole narrows, so GBHP and GFR fall back toward normal
response.why: Less pressure reaches the glomerulus, so filtration returns toward its set level. The juxtaglomerular cells also release less renin.

distractors.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinuses
distractors.why: Baroreceptors report arterial pressure to the brainstem. Tubuloglomerular feedback is local and needs no brain.

distractors.text: The efferent arteriole dilates
distractors.why: The response acts on the afferent arteriole. Widening the efferent arteriole would lower GBHP, but that is not what adenosine does here.

distractors.text: Juxtaglomerular cells release more renin
distractors.why: More NaCl at the macula densa lowers renin release. Renin rises when the macula densa senses too little NaCl.

distractors.text: Sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus
distractors.why: Sympathetic nerves can override autoregulation, but this loop works in a transplanted kidney that has lost its nerves.

loops.classify: The response (GFR falls back) opposes the stimulus (GFR rose), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A drug blocks the carrier the macula densa cells use to take up NaCl, so they sense almost none. What does this loop do?

options.text: It acts as if GFR were low: the afferent arteriole widens and renin release rises
options.why: Right. A sensor that reads "no NaCl" sends the signal for low GFR, so adenosine falls, the arteriole dilates and the juxtaglomerular cells release more renin.

options.text: It keeps GFR perfectly steady, because the myogenic mechanism takes over the loop
options.why: The myogenic mechanism is a separate loop in the same arteriole. It cannot read the tubular fluid for the macula densa.

options.text: It constricts the afferent arteriole hard, as if GFR were very high
options.why: Constriction needs the adenosine signal, which comes from NaCl uptake. With no uptake, the signal falls.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the macula densa is not part of the kidney’s control of GFR
options.why: The macula densa is the sensor of tubuloglomerular feedback, one of the two mechanisms of autoregulation.

loops.title: The myogenic mechanism: blood pressure rises
loops.scenario: A sudden fright makes your mean arterial pressure jump from 95 to 115 mm Hg for a minute. Within seconds, your GFR has barely changed.

stimulus.text: Arterial pressure rises and stretches the afferent arteriole wall
stimulus.why: The stimulus is the stretch of the vessel wall by higher pressure.

sensor.text: Mechanically gated channels in the arteriole’s smooth muscle
sensor.why: Stretch opens these channels in the membrane of the smooth muscle cells themselves.

afferent.text: No separate pathway: the channels are in the muscle cells themselves
afferent.why: The cells that sense the stretch are the cells that respond, so nothing has to carry the signal.

control.text: The smooth muscle cells, as calcium entering them sets their tension
control.why: Open channels let calcium in, and the calcium level inside decides how hard each cell contracts.

efferent.text: Calcium rising inside the same muscle cells
efferent.why: The command is chemical and stays inside the cell: calcium triggers contraction.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of the afferent arteriole
effector.why: The same muscle contracts and narrows the arteriole.

response.text: The afferent arteriole narrows, so GBHP and GFR stay near normal
response.why: More pressure is lost in the narrowed arteriole before blood reaches the glomerulus, cancelling the rise.

distractors.text: The efferent arteriole constricts
distractors.why: Efferent constriction would raise GBHP, adding to the rise instead of opposing it.

distractors.text: The cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata
distractors.why: The myogenic mechanism is local to the vessel. It works without any brain signal.

distractors.text: The macula densa senses more NaCl
distractors.why: That is tubuloglomerular feedback, the second, slightly slower mechanism of autoregulation.

loops.classify: The response (less pressure reaches the glomerulus) opposes the stimulus (more pressure arrived), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: Long-standing disease stiffens the afferent arterioles so their muscle can barely change their width. Blood pressure then rises from 100 to 140 mm Hg. What happens?

options.text: More of the higher pressure reaches the glomerulus, so GBHP and GFR rise
options.why: Right. The sensor still detects stretch, but the arteriole cannot narrow, so the rise passes straight through to the glomerulus.

options.text: GFR stays steady, because the stretch is still sensed
options.why: Sensing is not enough; the effector has to act. Here it cannot narrow the arteriole.

options.text: GFR falls, because a stiff arteriole blocks flow
options.why: A stiff arteriole that cannot constrict lets pressure through; it does not suddenly narrow.

options.text: The efferent arteriole takes over and narrows instead
options.why: Narrowing the efferent arteriole would raise GBHP further, not protect the glomerulus.

loops.title: Micturition: urine flow strengthens the contraction
loops.scenario: Once you start to urinate, the stream keeps going until the bladder is nearly empty, even though the bladder gets less stretched as it empties.

stimulus.text: Urine starts to flow through the urethra
stimulus.why: The stimulus for this loop is flow in the urethra, not stretch of the bladder wall.

sensor.text: Sensory receptors in the urethral wall
sensor.why: Sensory endings in the urethra fire as urine moves past them.

afferent.text: Sensory fibers to the sacral cord and on to the pons
afferent.why: Their signals travel into the spinal cord and up to the micturition centers.

control.text: The pontine and sacral micturition centers
control.why: The pons holds the switch in the voiding state, and the sacral center carries it out.

efferent.text: Parasympathetic fibers in the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2 to S4)
efferent.why: These fibers release acetylcholine onto the detrusor’s muscarinic receptor proteins.

effector.text: The detrusor muscle
effector.why: The bladder wall’s smooth muscle squeezes the bladder from all sides.

response.text: The detrusor contracts harder, pushing more urine through the urethra
response.why: More flow means more signal from the urethra, which drives a still stronger contraction until the bladder is nearly empty.

distractors.text: The external urethral sphincter contracts
distractors.why: Contracting the external sphincter stops flow and quiets the detrusor; it is how you hold on, not how emptying continues.

distractors.text: Sympathetic fibers from T11 to L2
distractors.why: Sympathetic output relaxes the detrusor and closes the internal sphincter: it serves storage, not emptying.

distractors.text: The pudendal nerve fires faster
distractors.why: The pudendal nerve keeps the external sphincter closed. Its firing falls during emptying.

loops.classify: The response (more flow) amplifies the stimulus (flow in the urethra), so this is positive feedback. It ends when the bladder is empty and flow stops.

failure.q: Injury to the sacral cord destroys the parasympathetic neurons to the bladder. What happens when the bladder fills?

options.text: The detrusor barely contracts, so the bladder overfills and dribbles
options.why: Right. With no parasympathetic drive the detrusor cannot squeeze, so urine builds up until pressure forces small amounts past the sphincters, and it dribbles.

options.text: The bladder empties at once whenever it fills, like an infant’s
options.why: Automatic emptying needs an intact sacral center to drive the detrusor; here its output neurons are lost.

options.text: The bladder empties normally, because the pons takes over the detrusor
options.why: The pons sends its commands through the sacral center. Without those neurons the command has no route to the detrusor.

options.text: The external sphincter opens, so urine leaks continuously while the bladder stays empty
options.why: The external sphincter depends on the pudendal nerve; losing the parasympathetic neurons leaves the detrusor too weak to empty the bladder.

loops.title: Pressure natriuresis: arterial pressure rises
loops.scenario: After a salty weekend, a man’s blood volume and arterial pressure creep up. Over the next day or two his kidneys excrete the extra salt and water, and his pressure settles back, even though his GFR has hardly changed.

stimulus.text: Arterial pressure reaching the kidney rises
stimulus.why: A higher pressure reaches the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta even when autoregulation protects the glomerulus.

sensor.text: The kidney tissue itself: the higher pressure reaches the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta and raises the pressure in the interstitial fluid around the tubules
sensor.why: No single sensory receptor is known. The pressure change is passed on through the kidney’s interstitial fluid, and local signals such as nitric oxide carry it to the tubule cells, which respond to it.

afferent.text: No nerve or hormone: the tubule cells respond where they sit
afferent.why: The mechanism works in an isolated kidney with every hormone and nerve held constant, so no pathway carries the signal elsewhere.

control.text: The proximal tubule cells, which set how many exchangers to keep in their apical membrane
control.why: The cells pull sodium–hydrogen exchangers out of the apical membrane when pressure rises.

efferent.text: Fewer sodium–hydrogen exchangers, and fluid leaking back between cells
efferent.why: Less sodium enters the cells, and some reabsorbed fluid leaks back into the tubule through the leaky tight junctions.

effector.text: The proximal tubule
effector.why: The segment that normally returns about two thirds of filtered sodium reabsorbs less.

response.text: More sodium and water are excreted, so blood volume and pressure fall
response.short: More Na+ and water out; pressure falls
response.why: Removing volume lowers arterial pressure back toward normal. Lower renin release adds to the effect in a whole person.

distractors.text: GFR rises steeply with the pressure
distractors.why: Within about 80 to 180 mm Hg, autoregulation holds GFR nearly steady. The extra excretion comes from reduced reabsorption, not more filtration.

distractors.text: Aldosterone release rises
distractors.why: Higher pressure lowers renin and so aldosterone. More aldosterone would keep sodium, the opposite response.

distractors.text: The collecting duct inserts more aquaporins
distractors.why: That is ADH’s action and would keep water, not excrete it.

loops.classify: The response (volume and pressure fall) opposes the stimulus (pressure rose), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: In long-standing high blood pressure, most researchers hold that this relationship has been reset. What does that mean for the loop?

options.text: It balances salt only at a higher pressure, so pressure stays high
options.why: Right. The loop still works, but around a higher set point: salt balance is reached only at a raised pressure.

options.text: The kidneys stop excreting sodium at any pressure
options.why: Then sodium would build up without limit. The loop still excretes the day’s salt, just at a higher pressure.

options.text: GFR rises with every rise in pressure instead
options.why: Resetting refers to the pressure needed for sodium excretion, not to the loss of GFR autoregulation.

options.text: The kidneys excrete more salt than normal at every pressure, so pressure falls
options.why: That would lower pressure, the opposite of what is seen in long-standing hypertension.

loops.title: Testosterone falls: the male HPG axis
loops.scenario: A man’s blood testosterone dips below its usual range. Within hours, his hypothalamus speeds its GnRH pulses, his pituitary releases more LH, and his testes bring testosterone back up.

stimulus.text: Blood testosterone falls below its set point
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is the level of testosterone in the blood.

sensor.text: Hypothalamic neurons and pituitary cells with androgen (and estrogen) receptor proteins
sensor.why: These cells read the testosterone level through androgen receptor proteins, and through estrogen receptor proteins after the brain converts some testosterone to estradiol. Less testosterone means a weaker brake.

afferent.text: Testosterone carried in the blood to the brain and pituitary
afferent.why: The information travels as the hormone level itself. No nerve reports it.

control.text: The hypothalamus, releasing GnRH in pulses
control.why: The hypothalamus sets the GnRH pulse rate, and the pulses set how much LH the pituitary releases.

efferent.text: GnRH in the portal vessels, then LH in the blood
efferent.why: GnRH reaches the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal vessels; LH then carries the command to the testes.

effector.text: Leydig (interstitial) cells of the testes
effector.why: LH binds receptor proteins on the Leydig cells between the tubules, which make testosterone from cholesterol.

response.text: Testosterone release rises back toward the set point
response.why: The response opposes the fall, and the rising testosterone then brakes GnRH and LH again.

distractors.text: Sertoli cells release inhibin
distractors.why: Inhibin is the brake on FSH in a separate arm of the axis. It does not make testosterone.

distractors.text: FSH acting on the Leydig cells
distractors.why: FSH acts on the Sertoli cells. LH is the hormone that drives the Leydig cells.

distractors.text: The posterior pituitary releases LH
distractors.why: LH comes from the anterior pituitary. The posterior pituitary releases only ADH and oxytocin.

loops.classify: The response (more testosterone) opposes the stimulus (low testosterone), and the restored level brakes GnRH and LH again, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: In androgen insensitivity, the androgen receptor protein does not work. What happens to LH and testosterone in an XY person with working testes?

options.text: Both are high
options.why: Right. The brain cannot read testosterone well, so it keeps signaling as if testosterone were low: LH rises and drives the Leydig cells to make even more testosterone, which the tissues still cannot use.

options.text: Both are low
options.why: That is the pattern of pituitary or hypothalamic failure, where nothing drives the testes. Here the pituitary is healthy and unbraked.

options.text: LH is high and testosterone is low
options.why: That is the pattern when the testes themselves fail. Here the testes work and respond to the extra LH.

options.text: Both are normal, because the loop does not need the sensor
options.why: The sensor is how the loop learns the testosterone level. Without it the brake is weak and the axis runs high.

loops.title: Inhibin and FSH: the second brake
loops.scenario: Sperm production in a man’s tubules slows for a while, and his Sertoli cells release less inhibin. His FSH creeps up, and the extra FSH drives the Sertoli cells to support spermatogenesis harder.

stimulus.text: Sertoli cell activity falls, so less inhibin enters the blood
stimulus.why: Inhibin from the Sertoli cells is the signal that reports how hard the tubules are working.

sensor.text: FSH-releasing cells of the anterior pituitary that respond to inhibin
sensor.why: Inhibin acts on the pituitary and lowers FSH release selectively, with little effect on LH. Less inhibin means a weaker brake.

afferent.text: Inhibin carried in the blood to the pituitary
afferent.why: Inhibin is a protein hormone, so the information travels in the blood.

control.text: The anterior pituitary, setting its FSH release
control.why: Inhibin works at the pituitary rather than the hypothalamus, so the pituitary decides how much FSH to release for each GnRH pulse.

efferent.text: FSH carried in the blood to the testes
efferent.why: FSH is the pituitary hormone that carries the command to the tubules.

effector.text: Sertoli (sustentacular) cells
effector.why: FSH binds receptor proteins on the Sertoli cells, which, with testosterone, support the developing sperm cells.

response.text: Spermatogenesis is supported more and inhibin release rises back
response.why: The Sertoli cells work harder and release more inhibin, which brakes FSH again.

distractors.text: Leydig cells release testosterone into the blood
distractors.why: That is the LH arm of the axis, braked mainly by testosterone itself, not by inhibin.

distractors.text: Inhibin brakes LH strongly
distractors.why: Inhibin lowers FSH selectively, with little effect on LH.

distractors.text: Androgen-binding protein releases testosterone
distractors.why: Androgen-binding protein holds testosterone inside the tubule; it does not release it or regulate FSH.

loops.classify: The response (more Sertoli activity and more inhibin) opposes the stimulus (low inhibin), so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: After some kinds of chemotherapy, the germ cells are destroyed but the Sertoli and Leydig cells survive. What hormone pattern results?

options.text: High FSH, normal LH and testosterone
options.why: Right. Sertoli cells with no germ cells to support release less inhibin, so FSH rises. The Leydig cells and their testosterone brake on LH are unaffected.

options.text: High FSH, high LH, low testosterone
options.why: That is the pattern when the whole testis fails, including the Leydig cells.

options.text: Low FSH, low LH, low testosterone
options.why: That is the pattern of pituitary or hypothalamic failure, not of lost germ cells.

options.text: Normal FSH, because FSH is set by testosterone alone
options.why: FSH has its own brake, inhibin, which is exactly what falls when germ cells are lost.

loops.title: The follicular phase: estradiol and inhibin hold FSH down
loops.scenario: As the old corpus luteum dies, its hormones fall and FSH climbs. A group of follicles grows, their estradiol and inhibin rise, and FSH falls again, leaving one follicle that can still grow.

stimulus.text: Estradiol and inhibin from the ovary fall
stimulus.why: When the corpus luteum dies, the ovarian hormones that were braking FSH fall.

sensor.text: Hypothalamic neurons and pituitary cells that respond to estradiol and inhibin
sensor.why: Estradiol acts through estrogen receptor proteins in both places; inhibin acts on the pituitary. Less of both means a weaker brake.

afferent.text: Estradiol and inhibin carried in the blood
afferent.why: The ovary reports its activity through its hormone levels. No nerve carries the message.

control.text: The hypothalamus (GnRH) and the anterior pituitary
control.why: GnRH pulses drive the pituitary, which sets how much FSH to release.

efferent.text: FSH carried in the blood to the ovaries
efferent.why: FSH is the command that reaches the follicles.

effector.text: Granulosa cells of the growing follicles
effector.why: FSH makes the granulosa cells multiply and switches on aromatase, which turns theca androgens into estradiol.

response.text: Follicles grow and release more estradiol and inhibin, so FSH falls again
response.why: The rising hormones restore the brake. As FSH falls, only the follicle most sensitive to it keeps growing.

distractors.text: High, sustained estradiol drives a surge of LH
distractors.why: That is the positive feedback of the days just before ovulation. Through most of the follicular phase, estradiol holds the gonadotropins down.

distractors.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum
distractors.why: Progesterone is the main brake in the luteal phase. Here the corpus luteum has died.

distractors.text: Theca cells convert androgens to estradiol
distractors.why: Theca cells make the androgens but lack aromatase; the granulosa cells do the conversion.

loops.classify: The response (more estradiol and inhibin) opposes the stimulus (low estradiol and inhibin) and lowers FSH again, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: At menopause, the ovaries have almost no follicles left. What happens to this loop?

options.text: FSH rises and stays high, because no follicles can answer it
options.why: Right. The pituitary keeps signaling, but no granulosa cells respond with estradiol and inhibin, so the brake never comes back. A high FSH is the laboratory sign of menopause.

options.text: FSH falls, because the pituitary stops working
options.why: The pituitary is healthy. It is the effector, the follicles, that is missing.

options.text: Estradiol rises, because FSH is high
options.why: Estradiol needs granulosa cells to make it. Without follicles, high FSH cannot raise it.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the hypothalamus runs the cycle alone
options.why: The loop needs follicles to answer FSH. Without them the whole cycle stops.

loops.title: The LH surge: estradiol switches to positive feedback
loops.scenario: Around day 12 of a 28-day cycle, the dominant follicle’s estradiol has stayed high for about two days. LH begins to shoot up, reaching many times its usual level about a day later, and ovulation follows about 34 to 36 hours after the rise began.

stimulus.text: Estradiol from the dominant follicle stays high for about two days
stimulus.why: Above roughly 200 pg/mL for about two days, estradiol’s effect on the brain and pituitary reverses from brake to accelerator.

sensor.text: Estrogen receptor proteins in hypothalamic neurons and pituitary cells
sensor.why: High sustained estradiol excites the estrogen-sensitive neurons that drive the GnRH neurons, and adds GnRH receptor proteins to the pituitary cells.

afferent.text: Estradiol carried in the blood
afferent.why: The dominant follicle reports its size and readiness through its estradiol output.

control.text: The hypothalamus (GnRH neurons and the neurons that drive them)
control.why: Estrogen-sensitive neurons that release kisspeptin drive the GnRH neurons, and GnRH output rises.

efferent.text: GnRH through the hypophyseal portal system
efferent.why: GnRH reaches the anterior pituitary through the portal vessels.

effector.text: Gonadotropin-making cells of the anterior pituitary
effector.why: Primed by estradiol with extra GnRH receptor proteins, each GnRH pulse releases far more LH.

response.text: An LH surge; before it, rising LH and FSH drove the follicle’s estradiol still higher
response.why: Before the surge, more LH and FSH made the dominant follicle release more estradiol, which pushed GnRH and LH higher again: the loop amplifies itself.

distractors.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum slows GnRH pulses
distractors.why: That is the luteal phase brake, after ovulation. There is no corpus luteum yet.

distractors.text: Low to moderate estradiol holds LH down
distractors.why: That is estradiol’s ordinary negative feedback, through most of the follicular phase. The surge needs estradiol high and sustained.

distractors.text: Inhibin raises FSH release
distractors.why: Inhibin lowers FSH; it does not drive the surge.

distractors.text: The posterior pituitary releases LH
distractors.why: LH comes from the anterior pituitary.

loops.classify: Before the surge, the response (more LH and FSH, so more estradiol) strengthens the stimulus (high estradiol), so this is positive feedback. It needs something to end it, and the surge sets up its own ending: the LH turns the follicle’s cells into a corpus luteum that makes mostly progesterone, so estradiol falls, the stimulus disappears, and ovulation follows.

failure.q: A woman takes the combined pill every day. Why does this loop never start?

options.text: No follicle dominates, so estradiol never stays high long enough
options.why: Right. Steady estrogen and progestin keep negative feedback on, FSH stays low, no follicle is selected, and the stimulus for positive feedback never appears. No surge, no ovulation.

options.text: The pill destroys the pituitary’s LH-making cells
options.why: The pituitary is unharmed; LH and FSH return within weeks of stopping the pill.

options.text: The pill blocks estrogen receptor proteins in the hypothalamus, so estradiol cannot be sensed
options.why: The pill contains an estrogen that acts on those receptor proteins. It works by keeping negative feedback switched on.

options.text: The surge happens, but the uterus ignores it
options.why: The LH surge acts on the follicle, not the uterus, and with the pill it does not happen at all.

loops.title: Plasma osmolality falls: ADH and thirst switch off
loops.scenario: At a summer picnic you drink 1.5 L of water in half an hour. Within the hour you are passing a lot of pale urine, you no longer want a drink, and by evening your plasma osmolality is back near 287 mOsm/kg.

stimulus.text: Plasma osmolality falls below its set point
stimulus.why: Absorbed water adds no solute, so it dilutes the plasma. The loop regulates concentration, holding plasma osmolality near 285 to 290 mOsm/kg.

sensor.text: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus swell and fire less
sensor.why: Water enters these sensory receptors from the dilute plasma, so they swell and their firing falls. A change of only 1 to 2% is enough.

afferent.text: Nerve connections within the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The osmoreceptors sit in the hypothalamus itself, so their signal travels only a short way, to the neurons that make ADH and to the thirst center.

control.text: The hypothalamus, including its ADH-making neurons and thirst center
control.why: The hypothalamus compares plasma osmolality with its set point and drives two responses at once: ADH release and thirst.

efferent.text: Less ADH released from the posterior pituitary, and the thirst signal switched off
efferent.why: The ADH-making neurons release less hormone from their endings in the posterior pituitary, so less reaches the kidneys in the blood; the thirst center stops driving you to drink.

effector.text: Principal cells of the collecting ducts, and your drinking behavior
effector.why: Two effectors both act on water: the kidneys decide how much water leaves, and drinking decides how much comes in.

response.text: Aquaporins are withdrawn, large volumes of dilute urine carry off the extra water, and you stop drinking, so plasma osmolality rises back to its set point
response.why: Without ADH the collecting ducts become nearly waterproof, so the extra water leaves as urine near 50 mOsm/L. Removing water raises osmolality, opposing the fall.

distractors.text: The adrenal cortex releases more aldosterone
distractors.why: Aldosterone controls the amount of sodium, which sets ECF volume. This loop corrects concentration by adding or removing water, not salt.

distractors.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria detect the fall in osmolality
distractors.why: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the atria sense blood volume, not concentration. Osmolality is sensed by osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus.

distractors.text: Principal cells insert more aquaporins into their apical membranes
distractors.why: More aquaporins would keep more water, diluting the plasma further. That is the response to a rise in osmolality.

distractors.text: The kidneys excrete extra sodium to restore the concentration
distractors.why: Losing sodium would lower osmolality even more. The loop fixes a dilute plasma by getting rid of water.

loops.classify: The response (water excreted, so osmolality rises) opposes the stimulus (osmolality falling), so this is negative feedback. As osmolality returns to the set point, the osmoreceptors return to their usual firing and ADH comes back up to its normal level.

failure.q: A lung tumor releases ADH on its own, whatever the plasma osmolality (SIADH). The person keeps drinking normal amounts. What happens after a large drink of water?

options.text: The water is kept: plasma osmolality keeps falling and cells, including brain cells, swell
options.why: Right. The osmoreceptors sense the fall and the hypothalamus cuts its own ADH, but the tumor’s ADH still reaches the principal cells, so their aquaporins stay in and the extra water cannot leave.

options.text: Nothing unusual happens, because the hypothalamus switches ADH off
options.why: The hypothalamus can only switch off its own ADH. The tumor’s ADH is outside the loop, so the efferent signal stays on.

options.text: The person becomes very thirsty and drinks even more
options.why: Thirst is still controlled by the osmoreceptors, and the plasma is dilute, so thirst is switched off. The problem is water kept, not water drunk.

options.text: Plasma osmolality rises, because the kidneys lose too much water
options.why: That happens when ADH is missing, as in diabetes insipidus. Here there is too much ADH, so water is kept.

loops.title: Blood pH falls from a fixed acid: breathing responds
loops.scenario: In untreated type 1 diabetes, ketone bodies pour into the blood faster than tissues can burn them. The hydrogen ions they release use up bicarbonate, and arterial pH starts to fall. Within minutes the person is breathing deeper and faster, and arterial PCO2 drifts down.

stimulus.text: Arterial H+ rises and pH falls, while PCO2 is still normal
stimulus.why: The acid uses up bicarbonate, so the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide falls below 20 and pH falls. The trigger here is a fixed acid, not carbon dioxide.

sensor.text: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies
sensor.why: The carotid bodies sense a fall in arterial pH within seconds, whatever the acid. The central chemoreceptors add little at first, because hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly.

afferent.text: Sensory neurons in the glossopharyngeal nerves
afferent.why: The glossopharyngeal nerves carry the carotid bodies’ signal to the medulla oblongata.

control.text: The respiratory centers in the medulla oblongata and pons
control.why: These groups of neurons set the rhythm, depth and rate of breathing, and they turn up their output as the carotid bodies fire faster.

efferent.text: Motor neurons in the phrenic and intercostal nerves
efferent.why: The phrenic nerves carry the command to the diaphragm, and the intercostal nerves to the intercostal muscles.

effector.text: The diaphragm and the intercostal muscles
effector.why: The breathing muscles contract harder and more often, raising alveolar ventilation.

response.text: Deeper, faster breathing blows off carbon dioxide, PCO2 falls, the bicarbonate buffer reaction takes up H+, and pH rises back toward normal
response.why: Lowering the bottom of the ratio to match the lower top moves the ratio back toward 20. The pH rises toward normal, though usually not all the way, and the bicarbonate stays low until the kidneys replace it.

distractors.text: Central chemoreceptors, which the acid reaches within seconds
distractors.why: Hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, so a fixed acid reaches the central chemoreceptors slowly. The fast response to a fixed acid comes from the carotid bodies.

distractors.text: Type A intercalated cells make new bicarbonate
distractors.why: The kidneys also defend pH, but over hours to days. This loop works in minutes, by changing breathing.

distractors.text: Breathing slows to keep more carbon dioxide in the blood
distractors.why: Keeping carbon dioxide would raise the bottom of the ratio and lower pH further, pushing the variable away from its set point.

distractors.text: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus
distractors.why: Baroreceptors sit near the carotid bodies but sense stretch from blood pressure, and they report to the cardiovascular center, not the respiratory centers.

loops.classify: The response (carbon dioxide breathed off, pH rising) opposes the stimulus (pH falling), so this is negative feedback. It is fast and strong but incomplete: it restores the ratio, not the lost bicarbonate.

failure.q: After surgery on both carotid arteries, a man has lost the function of both carotid bodies. Later he develops ketoacidosis. Compared with someone whose carotid bodies work, what happens in the first hours?

options.text: His breathing rises less, his PCO2 falls less, and his pH drops further
options.why: Right. The carotid bodies are the fast sensors of a fall in arterial pH. Without them, the central chemoreceptors respond only slowly, so less carbon dioxide is blown off and less of the pH change is offset.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the central chemoreceptors sense the acid just as fast
options.why: Hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the central chemoreceptors notice a fixed acid slowly.

options.text: He breathes faster than normal, because the respiratory centers are no longer held back
options.why: The carotid bodies drive breathing up; losing them removes drive, it does not release a brake.

options.text: His kidneys correct the pH within minutes instead
options.why: The kidneys take hours to start and 3 to 5 days to reach full strength. They cannot stand in for the lungs in the first hours.

loops.title: Plasma bicarbonate falls for days: the kidneys make new bicarbonate
loops.scenario: For a week a bodybuilder eats a very high-protein diet. The sulfuric acid from its amino acids keeps using up bicarbonate. His breathing barely changes, yet by the end of the week his plasma bicarbonate is steady again and his urine holds about twice its usual ammonium.

stimulus.text: Plasma bicarbonate and pH drift down as fixed acid uses up bicarbonate
stimulus.why: Sulfuric acid cannot be breathed out. Every H+ it adds uses up one bicarbonate, and only the kidneys can replace it.

sensor.text: Tubule cells whose own internal pH falls with the plasma
sensor.why: Acid in the plasma makes the fluid inside proximal tubule cells and intercalated cells more acidic too. The cells sense the change in themselves; no separate sensory receptor is involved.

afferent.text: None: the sensing cells are the responding cells
afferent.why: Because the tubule cells both sense and respond, no nerve or hormone has to carry the signal to them.

control.text: The same tubule cells, which change how many transport proteins and enzymes they run
control.why: Acid inside the cells speeds H+ secretion and the breakdown of glutamine into ammonium; alkali slows them.

efferent.text: Signals inside the cells that switch on more proton pumps and more glutamine breakdown
efferent.why: The command stays inside each cell, turning up the transport proteins and enzymes that secrete H+ and make ammonium.

effector.text: Proximal tubule cells and type A intercalated cells
effector.why: Proximal tubule cells make ammonium from glutamine; type A intercalated cells pump H+ into the urine, where it is carried away on phosphate and ammonia.

response.text: More H+ is excreted as titratable acid and ammonium, each one adding a new bicarbonate to the blood, so bicarbonate and pH rise back
response.why: Each H+ excreted leaves one bicarbonate behind in the tubule cell, which enters the blood. Over 3 to 5 days ammonium excretion rises, about twofold on a diet like this and up to five- to tenfold for a much larger acid load, so the daily acid is matched.

distractors.text: Type B intercalated cells secrete more bicarbonate into the urine
distractors.why: Excreting bicarbonate would lower plasma bicarbonate further. Type B cells are more active when the blood is too alkaline.

distractors.text: The lungs breathe out the sulfuric acid
distractors.why: Only carbon dioxide can leave through the lungs. Sulfuric acid is a fixed acid, and only the kidneys can excrete it.

distractors.text: Filtered bicarbonate is let through into the urine
distractors.why: Losing filtered bicarbonate would make the acid load worse. The kidneys reclaim nearly all of it.

loops.classify: The response (new bicarbonate added, pH rising) opposes the stimulus (bicarbonate and pH falling), so this is negative feedback. It is slow, taking 3 to 5 days to reach full strength, but it is the only defense that removes fixed acid from the body.

failure.q: A man takes acetazolamide, which blocks carbonic anhydrase in his tubule cells, while eating the same high-protein diet. What happens?

options.text: Less H+ is made and secreted, filtered bicarbonate is lost in the urine, and his plasma bicarbonate and pH fall further
options.why: Right. The tubule cells make the H+ they secrete from carbon dioxide and water with carbonic anhydrase. Blocked, they reclaim less filtered bicarbonate and add less new bicarbonate, so the acid load wins.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the proton pumps still work
options.why: The pumps can only move H+ that the cell has made, and carbonic anhydrase makes it.

options.text: His plasma bicarbonate rises, because less of it is used up in the cells
options.why: Carbonic anhydrase makes bicarbonate as well as H+ inside the cell; without it, less bicarbonate is reclaimed or made, and more is lost in the urine.

options.text: His urine becomes more acidic
options.why: With less H+ secreted and more bicarbonate left in the tubular fluid, the urine becomes more alkaline.

loops.title: Labor: cervical stretch and oxytocin
loops.map: Labor: oxytocin and uterine stretch (positive feedback)
loops.scenario: A woman is in the active phase of labor. Each contraction pushes the fetal head down onto her cervix, and over the next hours the contractions come harder and closer together until the baby is born.

stimulus.text: The fetal head presses down and stretches the cervix
stimulus.why: The variable that grows in this loop is stretch of the cervix and upper vagina, pushed by the head at each contraction.

sensor.text: Stretch-sensitive sensory receptors in the cervix and upper vagina
sensor.why: These mechanically gated endings fire faster the more the cervix is stretched.

afferent.text: Afferent nerve fibers up the spinal cord to the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The stretch signal travels as nerve impulses. This nerve-to-pituitary step is the Ferguson reflex.

control.text: Hypothalamic neurons whose axons end in the posterior pituitary
control.why: These neurons make oxytocin and decide when to release it; more stretch signals mean more frequent pulses.

efferent.text: Oxytocin released from the posterior pituitary into the blood in pulses
efferent.why: The command travels as a hormone. The hypothalamic axons release it straight into the blood in the posterior pituitary.

effector.text: Myometrium, rich in oxytocin receptor proteins and gap junctions at term
effector.why: Oxytocin binds its receptor proteins on the smooth muscle cells, releases calcium inside them through a G protein and IP3, and also makes the lining release prostaglandins. Gap junctions spread each contraction across the wall.

response.text: Stronger contractions push the head down harder, stretching the cervix further
response.why: The response adds to the stimulus: a harder contraction means more stretch, which means more oxytocin and a harder contraction still.

distractors.text: Oxytocin released from the anterior pituitary
distractors.why: Oxytocin is made by hypothalamic neurons and released from their axon endings in the posterior pituitary. The anterior pituitary releases hormones such as prolactin and LH.

distractors.text: Progesterone from the placenta keeps the myometrium quiet
distractors.why: Progesterone opposes contraction; losing its effect near term lets labor happen. It is not part of the loop that strengthens contractions.

distractors.text: Contractions weaken as the cervix stretches, so labor settles at a set point
distractors.why: That would be negative feedback. In this loop stretch makes contractions stronger, so there is no set point to settle at.

distractors.text: Prolactin released into the blood
distractors.why: Prolactin drives milk production after birth. It does not make the myometrium contract.

loops.classify: The response (stronger contractions) increases the stimulus (stretch of the cervix), so this is positive feedback. It does not settle at a set point; it ends only when an outside event breaks it: the baby is born, the stretch stops, and the afferent signals stop.

failure.q: A woman whose posterior pituitary was damaged years ago releases very little oxytocin. She goes into labor at term. What is the most likely course?

options.text: Labor can start and progress, but contractions cannot build up through this loop
options.why: Right. The loop strengthens contractions; it is not what starts labor, and a synthetic oxytocin drip can strengthen them if needed. Women with very little oxytocin have had normal spontaneous labors, because prostaglandins, gap junctions and the loss of progesterone’s effect also drive contractions.

options.text: Labor can never start, because a rise in blood oxytocin is what begins every labor
options.why: Blood oxytocin barely rises before labor. The start of labor depends on changes in the uterus, cervix and placenta, such as functional progesterone withdrawal and placental CRH.

options.text: Contractions grow stronger than usual, because nothing limits the loop
options.why: Oxytocin is the loop’s command. Without it the loop cannot strengthen the contractions at all, let alone more than usual.

options.text: The cervix stops sensing stretch
options.why: The sensory receptors and afferent nerves are untouched. Stretch is still sensed; the hormone that carries the command is missing.

loops.title: A cold newborn: brown fat
loops.scenario: A term baby is born wet into a room about 10 °C cooler than the uterus. Its temperature starts to fall, and within minutes its brown fat is making heat.

stimulus.text: Skin and body temperature fall as the wet newborn loses heat
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is body temperature. Evaporation from wet skin and a large surface for its size make a newborn lose heat fast.

sensor.text: Cold-sensing thermoreceptors in the skin
sensor.why: Cold-sensing endings in the skin fire more as the skin cools, the first place the heat loss shows.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carrying cold signals to the hypothalamus
afferent.why: The temperature information reaches the brain as nerve impulses along sensory pathways.

control.text: The hypothalamus, comparing temperature with its set point
control.why: The hypothalamus is the body’s thermostat; when temperature is below its set point it raises heat production.

efferent.text: Sympathetic nerves releasing norepinephrine onto brown fat
efferent.why: The command to make heat reaches brown fat through sympathetic nerves; norepinephrine binds beta receptor proteins on the fat cells.

effector.text: Brown adipose tissue between the shoulder blades and around the neck, kidneys and great vessels
effector.why: Brown fat cells break down their fat and run their mitochondria with a channel protein that lets H+ leak back, so the energy leaves as heat instead of ATP.

response.text: Nonshivering thermogenesis adds heat, and body temperature rises back toward the set point
response.why: The heat opposes the fall that set the loop off. As temperature is restored, the cold signals fade and heat production eases.

distractors.text: Vigorous shivering of the skeletal muscles
distractors.why: A newborn’s shivering is weak and adds little heat. Brown fat, not shivering, is its main defense.

distractors.text: Parasympathetic nerves releasing acetylcholine onto brown fat
distractors.why: Brown fat is driven by the sympathetic division and norepinephrine, not by parasympathetic nerves.

distractors.text: Sweat glands release more sweat
distractors.why: Sweating sheds heat. In the cold the body cuts heat loss and makes heat; it does not sweat.

loops.classify: The response (heat from brown fat) opposes the stimulus (falling temperature), bringing it back toward the set point, so this is negative feedback.

failure.q: A baby born at 30 weeks has much less brown fat and a thinner layer of fat under the skin than a term baby. In the same cool room, what happens to its temperature?

options.text: It falls faster and further, because the effector makes too little heat
options.why: Right. The sensor, nerves and hypothalamus work, but the effector is small, and less insulation lets heat escape faster. That is why preterm babies are dried, covered and kept warm at once.

options.text: It stays steady, because the hypothalamus makes the skeletal muscles shiver hard enough instead
options.why: A newborn’s shivering is weak, and a preterm baby’s even weaker. It cannot make up for the missing brown fat.

options.text: It rises, because a smaller baby loses less heat
options.why: A smaller baby has even more surface for its size, so it loses heat faster, not slower.

options.text: It falls only if the thermoreceptors fail
options.why: The thermoreceptors work. The loop fails at the effector, which cannot make enough heat to answer them.

loops.title: Too warm: the skin sheds heat
loops.map: Body temperature: too hot and too cold
loops.scenario: You hike uphill for an hour on a warm, dry day. Your skin flushes, sweat beads on your forehead and dries in the breeze, and your body temperature rises a little and then holds steady.

stimulus.text: Heat from working muscles and warm air raises body temperature above its set point
stimulus.why: The regulated variable is body temperature. Your muscles are releasing heat faster than you are losing it.

sensor.text: Warm-sensitive nerve endings in the skin and temperature-sensitive neurons in the brain
sensor.why: Free nerve endings in the skin that respond to warmth fire faster as the skin warms, and neurons in the brain sense the temperature of the blood around them.

afferent.text: Sensory nerves carrying signals from the skin to the brain
afferent.why: The afferent pathway carries the information from the skin toward the control center.

control.text: The brain’s temperature control center
control.why: The control center compares the incoming temperature signals with the set point and, finding the body too warm, sends out heat-loss commands.

efferent.text: Nerve signals to the dermal blood vessels and the eccrine sweat glands
efferent.short: Nerves to dermal vessels, sweat glands
efferent.why: The commands travel as nerve signals. In most (hairy) skin they actively relax the vessel walls; in the palms, soles and lips the vessels widen mainly as the steady signal that keeps them narrowed eases.

effector.text: Smooth muscle of the dermal vessels, and the eccrine sweat glands
effector.why: The smooth muscle relaxes so the vessels widen, and the eccrine sweat glands secrete watery sweat onto the skin surface.

response.text: Dermal blood flow rises and sweat evaporates, so more heat leaves and body temperature falls back toward the set point
response.why: Warm blood near the surface loses heat by radiation and convection, and each liter of sweat that evaporates removes about 580 kcal. Both oppose the rise.

distractors.text: Arrector pili muscles contract to raise goose bumps
distractors.why: Goose bumps are part of the response to cold, and in humans they hold almost no extra heat in anyway.

distractors.text: Apocrine sweat glands in the armpits release more secretion
distractors.why: Apocrine glands respond to emotional stress, pain and sexual arousal, not to heat. Heat loss by sweating is the eccrine glands’ job.

distractors.text: Skeletal muscles shiver
